source_title: Efficacy and safety of semaglutide on weight loss in obese or overweight patients without diabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
research_question: In randomized trials of adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes, how did semaglutide compare with placebo for adverse events, serious adverse events, discontinuation due to adverse events, and common gastrointestinal events?
claim_text: The meta-analysis reported higher pooled risks with semaglutide than placebo for adverse events, serious adverse events, discontinuation due to adverse events, nausea, and diarrhea, while hypoglycemia did not differ.
population: Adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes in semaglutide randomized controlled trials; six studies (4,512 participants) contributed adverse-event and serious-adverse-event data, and eight studies (4,567 participants) contributed discontinuation-due-to-adverse-event data.
intervention: Subcutaneous semaglutide across included trial doses and durations.
comparator: Placebo.
outcome: Any adverse event, serious adverse event, adverse event leading to discontinuation, nausea, diarrhea, and hypoglycemia.
result_summary: Compared with placebo, pooled risk ratios were 1.10 (95% CI 1.05 to 1.16) for adverse events, 1.34 (1.10 to 1.65) for serious adverse events, and 2.29 (1.74 to 3.01) for adverse events leading to discontinuation. Nausea RR was 2.58 (2.33 to 2.86) and diarrhea RR was 2.01 (1.79 to 2.27); hypoglycemia did not differ (RR 0.94, 0.66 to 1.34).
short_source_excerpt: Combined statistics noted that semaglutide increased the incidences of AEs, SAEs, and DAEs compared with placebo, especially DAEs
limitations: The any-adverse-event analysis had high heterogeneity (I2=82%), reflecting variation across included studies.
Included trials varied in semaglutide dose, treatment duration, and population details; pooled estimates are not one uniform 2.4 mg regimen or treatment window.
The review included a limited number of studies and divided one study into seven separate trials for analyses, which the authors noted could affect homogeneity and publication bias.
Aggregate event incidence does not preserve event timing, recurrence, severity within each category, or individual benefit-harm tradeoffs.
The review predates later semaglutide trials and cannot provide a complete current class-wide safety assessment.
uncertainty_notes: This record qualifies weight-loss efficacy with pooled tolerability and discontinuation findings from the same review. It does not compute a benefit-harm balance, establish causality for every event, or generalize to all GLP-1 receptor agonists.
confidence_note: High confidence that the extracted pooled estimates match the source; this is not a clinical safety rating or a confidence score for individual treatment decisions.

source_title: Laparoscopic gastric banding with liraglutide and type 2 diabetes: a randomised placebo-controlled trial (GLIDE)
research_question: In adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes after laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding, did six months of liraglutide 1.8 mg improve body weight compared with placebo?
claim_text: In the underpowered GLIDE pilot, adding liraglutide 1.8 mg after gastric banding did not improve body weight versus placebo at six months; at 12 months, six months after treatment ended, adjusted body weight was higher in the former liraglutide arm.
population: 27 adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes randomized after laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding; 13 received liraglutide and 14 received placebo.
intervention: Subcutaneous liraglutide 1.8 mg once daily for six months after laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding.
comparator: Placebo for six months after laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding.
outcome: Between-group body-weight difference at six months and at 12 months, six months after investigational treatment ended; body weight was a secondary outcome.
result_summary: At six months, adjusted body weight did not differ between groups (difference 2.0 kg, 95% CI -4.2 to 8.1; p=0.50). At 12 months, adjusted body weight was 8.2 kg higher in the former liraglutide arm (95% CI 1.6 to 14.9; p=0.02). The trial randomized 27 participants against a planned sample of 58 and was significantly underpowered.
short_source_excerpt: There was no difference between arms in weight at 6 months
limitations: The pilot randomized 27 participants rather than the planned 58 and was underpowered for its primary and secondary outcomes.
The intervention was liraglutide 1.8 mg rather than semaglutide 2.4 mg, so this result cannot be treated as a direct semaglutide comparison.
Participants had type 2 diabetes and had undergone laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding, a materially different population and treatment context from STEP 5.
Body weight was a secondary outcome; the primary outcome was HbA1c.
The 12-month result occurred six months after investigational treatment ended and is not an on-treatment efficacy comparison.
The small sample and missing follow-up observations limit precision and generalizability.
uncertainty_notes: This record qualifies broad GLP-1 receptor agonist weight expectations after metabolic surgery. It does not contradict semaglutide-versus-placebo efficacy in non-surgical adults without diabetes, establish a liraglutide class effect, or determine why the 12-month groups differed.

source_title: The DEPRE'5 study: pragmatic, multicentre, five-arm, parallel-group randomised controlled trial with blinded assessment to compare treatment strategies in major depression after a failed selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor treatment
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a five-arm, blinded-assessment randomized controlled trial (DEPRE'5, EudraCT No. 2007-002130-11), MDD patients unresponsive to an initial SSRI achieved higher response rates and greater depressive-symptom-severity reduction with alternative second-line strategies (lithium augmentation, nortriptyline combination, switching to venlafaxine, or adding problem-solving therapy) than with simple SSRI dose optimization.
population: 257 adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) unresponsive to an initial SSRI, randomized across 5 arms: SSRI dose optimization (n=51), lithium augmentation (n=46), nortriptyline combination (n=48), switch to venlafaxine (n=55), and SSRI plus problem-solving therapy (n=57).
intervention: Four alternative second-line strategies after SSRI non-response: lithium augmentation, nortriptyline combination, switching to venlafaxine (an SNRI), or adding problem-solving therapy to the existing SSRI.
comparator: SSRI dose optimization (continuing/increasing the dose of the original SSRI).
outcome: Week-6 response and remission rates (primary), assessed by blinded evaluators using the 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS-17); change in HDRS-17 score (secondary).
result_summary: Pooled across the four alternative strategies, response was higher than with SSRI dose optimization (28.2% vs 14.3%; odds ratio 2.36, 95% CI [1.0, 5.6], p=0.05), with greater HDRS-17 score reduction (-2.6 points, 95% CI [-4.9, -0.4], p=0.021). Remission was numerically higher but not statistically significant (16.9% vs 12.2%; OR 1.46, 95% CI [0.57, 3.71], p=0.27). Individually, switching to venlafaxine (OR 2.53, 95% CI [0.94, 6.80], p=0.067; HDRS-17 difference -2.7, 95% CI [-5.5, 0.0], p=0.054) and SSRI-plus-problem-solving-therapy (OR 2.46, 95% CI [0.92, 6.62], p=0.074; HDRS-17 difference -3.1, 95% CI [-5.8, -0.3], p=0.032) showed the most consistent effects among the four alternative arms.

source_span.locator_note: The response/remission odds ratios and HDRS-17 differences this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: Alternative second-line strategies led to higher response (28.2% v. 14.3%, odds ratio = 2.36 [95% CI 1.0-5.6], p = 0.05) ... with greater HDRS-17 score reductions (-2.6 [95% CI -4.9 to -0.4], p = 0.021]) than SSRI-Opt.
limitations: The trial's own conclusion notes 'limited statistical power'; several individual-arm comparisons (e.g. venlafaxine's response-rate OR, both alternative arms' remission effects) reached only marginal or non-significance (p=0.05-0.27).

The five arms are not all pharmacologically comparable (one arm adds psychotherapy rather than a medication change), so this record's pooled 'alternative strategies vs SSRI-Opt' comparison combines heterogeneous intervention types.
This is a second-line (post-SSRI-failure) population, not treatment-naive MDD patients, so results should not be generalized to first-line SSRI/SNRI efficacy.
Nortriptyline combination showed the most adverse effects (75% vs 28.1% in SSRI+PST, p<0.01), a safety trade-off this record's efficacy-focused summary does not fully capture.
This record does not independently assess randomization integrity, blinding adequacy, or missing-data handling beyond what the abstract reports.
uncertainty_notes: This record qualifies the corpus's core question by addressing a specific, clinically important subpopulation: patients who have already failed an SSRI. It directly supports the venlafaxine (SNRI) switch strategy specifically with real HDRS-17 data, and should be read alongside first-line SSRI/SNRI efficacy records in this corpus rather than as a general statement about SSRI/SNRI efficacy from treatment initiation.
confidence_note: High confidence that the extracted result is relevant to the research question and source-linked; not a confidence score for the scientific conclusion or corpus-level answer.

source_title: Escitalopram versus other antidepressive agents for major depressive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: A meta-analysis of 30 randomized controlled trials found escitalopram significantly more effective than citalopram (another SSRI) for acute response and remission in major depressive disorder, though escitalopram did not differ significantly from other antidepressants in early or follow-up response.
population: Adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) enrolled in 30 randomized controlled trials comparing escitalopram against another antidepressant (16 trials vs another SSRI, 14 trials vs a newer antidepressant), identified via search of Medline/PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and ClinicalTrials.gov through July 2023.
intervention: Escitalopram (SSRI).
comparator: Other antidepressants, including citalopram (another SSRI) and other newer antidepressant agents.
outcome: Acute-phase treatment response and remission, calculated on an intention-to-treat basis; risk ratios (dichotomous data) and standardized mean differences (continuous data) with 95% confidence intervals, random-effects model.
result_summary: Escitalopram was significantly more effective than citalopram in achieving acute response (risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI [0.50, 0.87]) and remission (risk ratio 0.53, 95% CI [0.30, 0.93]). source_title: A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing the Effects of Vilazodone, Escitalopram, and Vortioxetine Monotherapy on Metabolic Parameters in Patients With Major Depressive Disorder
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a three-arm randomized controlled trial, vilazodone, escitalopram (an SSRI), and vortioxetine monotherapy each substantially reduced depressive symptom severity over 16 weeks in adults with major depressive disorder, including those with comorbid type 2 diabetes, with no statistically significant between-drug difference in the degree of symptom reduction.
population: 96 adults with major depressive disorder who completed a 16-week, three-arm, randomized, open-label trial (of 134 screened, 119 eligible, 96 in the per-protocol population); mean age 46.3 +/- 6.2 years; stratified into diabetic and non-diabetic subgroups. Registered in the Clinical Trial Registry of India (CTRI/2022/07/043808).
intervention: Vilazodone (20-40 mg/day) or vortioxetine (5-20 mg/day) monotherapy.
comparator: Escitalopram (10-20 mg/day, an SSRI), used as the active control arm.
outcome: Change in 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS-17) score from baseline to 16 weeks; metabolic indices (fasting blood sugar, HbA1c, lipid profile, hepatic parameters, serum creatinine) as secondary outcomes.
result_summary: Median baseline HDRS score was 30.0 across all three groups (p=0.964, no significant baseline difference). At 16 weeks, median HDRS scores had dropped to 15.0 (vilazodone), 14.0 (escitalopram), and 13.0 (vortioxetine). Post hoc analysis showed no statistically significant between-group differences in HDRS reduction or in most metabolic parameters, except for reductions in glycemic indices specifically among diabetic patients.

source_span.locator_note: The baseline and 16-week HDRS scores this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: Across all study groups, the median baseline HDRS score was 30.0 (p = 0.964). At 16 weeks, the equivalent scores dropped to 15.0, 14.0, and 13.0 (p = 0.002)... The post hoc analysis manifested no statistically significant changes between any parameters.
limitations: Open-label design (not blinded), which can inflate apparent symptom improvement relative to placebo-controlled or blinded trials.
Small per-arm sample size (approximately 32 per arm within the 96-patient per-protocol population), limiting power to detect true between-drug differences.

The abstract's p=0.002 figure is ambiguous as extracted -- it is not fully clear from the abstract text alone whether this refers to the within-group change over time or a between-group comparison at 16 weeks; this record reports the values as stated without resolving that ambiguity, and notes the abstract's own explicit statement that post hoc analysis found no significant between-group differences.
This record does not independently assess dropout/attrition patterns (23 of 119 eligible participants did not complete the per-protocol population) or their potential effect on the reported results.
This is a single trial from a single registry region (India); generalizability to other populations is not independently assessed here.
uncertainty_notes: This record directly supports the corpus's core question with real HDRS-17 symptom-severity data for escitalopram (an SSRI), while also providing head-to-head context against vilazodone and vortioxetine (non-SSRI/SNRI serotonergic agents) and diabetes-comorbidity context. The apparent large within-arm symptom reduction (HDRS ~30 to ~13-15) should not be read as isolating drug effect from open-label/regression-to-the-mean effects, which this uncontrolled-for-placebo design cannot rule out.

source_title: Agomelatine as adjunctive therapy with SSRIs or SNRIs for major depressive disorder: a multicentre, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In an 8-week, multicentre, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adding agomelatine to ongoing SSRI or SNRI treatment did not significantly improve depressive-symptom reduction, remission, or response over adding placebo, in MDD patients with inadequate SSRI/SNRI response.
population: 123 adults with MDD who had an inadequate response to SSRI or SNRI treatment lasting at least 2 weeks; 60 randomized to agomelatine augmentation, 63 to placebo augmentation, both added to continued SSRI/SNRI treatment.
intervention: Agomelatine added to ongoing SSRI or SNRI treatment.
comparator: Placebo added to ongoing SSRI or SNRI treatment.
outcome: Primary: HAMD-17 total score at week 8. Secondary: HAMD-17 at weeks 2 and 4, remission and response rates over 8 weeks, self-rated depression/anxiety/anhedonia/sleep/social/cognitive functioning, and adverse events.
result_summary: The between-group difference in HAMD-17 reduction from baseline to week 8 was not significant (adjusted difference in means -0.12, 95% CI [-3.94, 3.70], p=0.90, Cohen's d=-0.022). Remission occurred in 30/60 (50.0%) of the agomelatine group vs 33/63 (52.3%) of the placebo group (OR 0.88, 95% CI [0.42, 1.85], p=0.74). Response occurred in 36/60 (60.0%) vs 41/63 (65.2%) (OR 0.85, 95% CI [0.40, 1.80], p=0.68). No secondary outcome (HAMD-17 at weeks 2/4, PHQ-9, HAMA, GAD-7, CGI severity, SHAPS, SDS, or cognitive-function measures) reached statistical significance between groups. Agomelatine was generally well tolerated with a safety profile comparable to placebo.

source_span.section: Table 2 (Primary outcomes, secondary outcomes and safety)
source_span.locator_note: The HAMD-17 adjusted mean difference and the remission/response counts and odds ratios this record centers on appear in Table 2 on page 8 of the local PDF; the null top-line result is also stated in the structured Abstract's Results/Conclusions on page 1.

short_source_excerpt: HAMD-17 at week 8: Agomelatine+SSRI/SNRI 7.2 (5.2), n=60; Placebo+SSRI/SNRI 7.4 (6.3), n=63; adjusted difference in means -0.12 (-3.94 to 3.70), p=0.90. Response: 36 (60.0%) vs 41 (65.2%), OR 0.85 (0.40-1.80).
limitations: This is an augmentation-trial population (SSRI/SNRI non-responders), not treatment-naive MDD patients, so the null result speaks to agomelatine add-on value specifically, not to SSRI/SNRI first-line efficacy itself.

A null result on the primary endpoint does not establish that agomelatine augmentation is ineffective for all subgroups; the trial was powered (80% power, Cohen's d=0.52) for a medium effect size, so smaller true effects could be missed.
This record does not independently assess randomization integrity, blinding adequacy, or missing-data handling beyond what the paper reports.
The trial evaluates agomelatine as an adjunct, not SSRI/SNRI monotherapy, so it is evidence about augmentation strategy choice, not about the base SSRI/SNRI treatment's own efficacy.
uncertainty_notes: This record is a genuine negative/null RCT result and is included specifically for that reason: it should be read alongside this corpus's positive-result records (e.g. DEPRE'5's venlafaxine-switch and SSRI+PST arms) as evidence that not every second-line augmentation strategy after SSRI/SNRI non-response shows benefit -- agomelatine augmentation did not, in this trial.

source_title: The safety and efficacy of escitalopram and sertraline in post-stroke depression: a randomized controlled trial
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a randomized controlled trial in post-stroke depression (PSD) patients, escitalopram produced greater depressive-symptom reduction than sertraline, with a faster onset of effect and a lower incidence of adverse effects, though overall response rate did not differ significantly between the two SSRIs.
population: 60 adults (aged 40-89) with an ICD-10 diagnosis of post-stroke depression (PSD), randomized 1:1 to escitalopram (n=30) or sertraline (n=30), registered as ChiCTR1800017373.
intervention: Escitalopram, flexibly dosed 10-20 mg/day, titrated over 2 weeks.
comparator: Sertraline, flexibly dosed 50-200 mg/day, titrated over 2 weeks.
outcome: HAMD-24 and HAMA-14 scores at baseline and 1, 3, 4, 6, and 8 weeks; overall response rate (>=50% HAMD-24 reduction); adverse-effect incidence (via TESS); cognitive function (MOCA) and daily-living ability (ADL) at 8 weeks.
result_summary: HAMD-24 scores decreased significantly in both groups over the 8-week follow-up, with a statistically significant between-group difference favoring escitalopram (F=4.068, p<0.05); the difference was already significant at the end of week 1 (T=2.620, p<0.05), indicating faster onset. HAMA-14 anxiety scores decreased in both groups with no significant between-group difference (F=3.185, p>0.05). Overall response rate did not differ significantly between groups (chi-squared=3.042, p>0.05). Adverse-effect incidence was significantly lower in the escitalopram group (chi-squared=9.097, p<0.05). Cognitive function (MOCA, Z=1.040, p>0.05) and daily-living recovery (ADL, Z=0.143, p>0.05) improved comparably between groups.

source_span.section: Results (Comparison of HAMD-24/HAMA-14 scores; Clinical efficacy; Adverse effects)
source_span.locator_note: The F-statistics, p-values, and chi-squared test results this record centers on appear in the body-text Results section on pages 4-5 of the local PDF; the paper does not report raw per-group response-rate percentages in extractable text, only the significance tests.

short_source_excerpt: escitalopram showed superior efficacy in alleviating depression symptoms compared to sertraline (F = 4.068, p < 0.05)... the overall response rate showed no significance between the TC and CG, while the incidence of adverse effects was lower in patients receiving escitalopram intervention.
limitations: Small sample size (n=30 per arm) from a single center, explicitly flagged by the authors as needing replication in larger cohorts.

Population is specifically post-stroke depression in an older cohort (median age ~67), a comorbid population, not general-population MDD -- findings should not be generalized to first-line SSRI choice outside this context without caution.

The paper reports significance tests (F, T, chi-squared statistics and p-values) rather than raw per-group response-rate percentages in the extractable text, limiting the precision of this record's effect-size reporting.
This record does not independently assess randomization integrity, blinding adequacy, or missing-data handling beyond what the paper reports; 2 patients per arm withdrew before completion.
uncertainty_notes: This record qualifies the corpus's core question with a head-to-head SSRI-vs-SSRI comparison (escitalopram vs sertraline) in a specific comorbid population (post-stroke depression), rather than either drug vs placebo. It should be read as evidence for relative within-class efficacy/tolerability differences, not as a general statement that SSRIs as a class outperform or underperform SNRIs.

source_title: Antidepressants available in Japan for older people with major depressive disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a systematic review and pairwise meta-analysis of double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials of antidepressants available in Japan (including the SSRIs escitalopram and sertraline, and the SNRI venlafaxine, among others) for older adults with MDD, antidepressants as a class significantly outperformed placebo on response and symptom-severity improvement, but were also associated with significantly higher discontinuation due to adverse events.
population: Older adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) enrolled across 9 double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials (n=2,145 total); no trial was conducted in Japan, but all evaluated antidepressants available in the Japanese market.
intervention: Antidepressants available in Japan, including duloxetine, escitalopram, imipramine, sertraline, venlafaxine, and vortioxetine.
comparator: Placebo.
outcome: Response rate (primary), depressive symptom scale score improvement, remission rate, all-cause discontinuation, discontinuation due to adverse events, and incidence of at least one adverse event.
result_summary: Antidepressants had significantly higher response rates than placebo (RR 1.38, 95% CI [1.04, 1.83], p=0.02) and significantly greater improvement in depressive symptom scale scores (SMD -0.62, 95% CI [-0.92, -0.33], p<0.0001). However, antidepressants were associated with significantly higher discontinuation due to adverse events (RR 1.94, 95% CI [1.30, 2.88], p=0.001) and a significantly higher incidence of at least one adverse event (RR 1.11, 95% CI [1.02, 1.21], p=0.02) versus placebo. Groups did not differ significantly on remission rate or all-cause discontinuation. The authors concluded antidepressants available in Japan are only weakly recommended for moderate-to-severe MDD in older adults, given the efficacy-tolerability trade-off.

source_span.locator_note: The response-rate, symptom-improvement, and discontinuation risk ratios this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: Antidepressants have significantly higher response rates than placebo (RR [95% CI] = 1.38 [1.04, 1.83], p = 0.02)... antidepressants were associated with a higher discontinuation rate due to adverse events (RR [95% CI] = 1.94 [1.30, 2.88], p = 0.001).
limitations: Population is specifically older adults (age criteria vary by included trial), an age-restricted subgroup, not general-population MDD -- findings should not be generalized to younger adult SSRI/SNRI efficacy without caution.

The meta-analysis pools multiple distinct antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRI, TCA, and others) rather than isolating SSRI/SNRI-specific effects, so the pooled response-rate and discontinuation risk ratios should not be attributed to any single agent or class without checking the paper's per-drug subgroup analyses.

Only 9 trials (n=2,145) were available for this older-adult population, a comparatively small evidence base for a meta-analysis, which the authors' own conclusion ('only weakly recommended') reflects.
This record does not independently assess the meta-analysis's study-selection criteria, heterogeneity statistics, or publication-bias assessment beyond what the abstract reports.
uncertainty_notes: This record supports the corpus's core question at the class level (antidepressants including SSRIs/SNRIs reduce depressive symptoms more than placebo) while also surfacing a real efficacy-tolerability trade-off in older adults specifically -- it should be read as evidence-synthesis-level support with an important population-specific caveat, not as an unqualified endorsement.

source_title: Efficacy and safety of aticaprant, a kappa receptor antagonist, adjunctive to oral SSRI/SNRI antidepressant in major depressive disorder: results of a phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a phase 2, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, adding aticaprant (a kappa opioid receptor antagonist) to ongoing SSRI/SNRI treatment produced a significantly greater reduction in depressive symptoms than adding placebo, in MDD patients with an inadequate response to their SSRI/SNRI.
population: 184 adults (18-64) with moderate-to-severe MDD (MADRS >= 25) and inadequate response to an ongoing antidepressant for 6 weeks to 12 months; 169 included in safety analyses (aticaprant n=85, placebo n=84), 166 in full intent-to-treat efficacy analyses, and 121 placebo lead-in non-responders in the enriched intent-to-treat analysis.
intervention: Aticaprant 10 mg once daily, added to ongoing SSRI/SNRI treatment, for 6 weeks.
comparator: Placebo added to ongoing SSRI/SNRI treatment.
outcome: MADRS (Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale) total score change from baseline at week 6; treatment-emergent adverse events.
result_summary: Aticaprant significantly improved MADRS total score versus placebo at week 6 in both analysis populations: enriched intent-to-treat (least squares mean difference -2.1, upper limit 1-sided 80% CI -1.09, 1-sided p=0.044, effect size 0.23) and full intent-to-treat (-3.1, upper limit 2.21, 1-sided p=0.002, effect size 0.36). The between-group difference was larger among participants with higher baseline anhedonia (Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale score >= baseline median). Most common treatment-emergent adverse events for aticaprant vs placebo were headache (11.8% vs 7.1%), diarrhea (8.2% vs 2.4%), nasopharyngitis (5.9% vs 2.4%), and pruritus (5.9% vs 0%); discontinuation due to adverse events was low and similar between arms (1.2% each).

source_span.locator_note: The MADRS least-squares mean differences, confidence limits, p-values, and adverse-event rates this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: Improvement... in MADRS total score at week 6 for aticaprant was significant versus placebo (eITT: -2.1 [-1.09], 1-sided p = 0.044; effect size (ES) 0.23; fITT -3.1 [2.21], 1-sided p = 0.002; ES 0.36).
limitations: This is an augmentation-trial population (SSRI/SNRI inadequate responders), not treatment-naive MDD patients, so the result speaks to aticaprant add-on value specifically, not to SSRI/SNRI first-line efficacy itself.

The trial uses 1-sided p-values and confidence limits (a pre-specified phase 2 design choice), which is a less conservative statistical convention than the 2-sided intervals used elsewhere in this corpus -- readers comparing effect sizes across records should account for this.
A phase 2 study with a 6-week duration and enriched-population analysis (excluding placebo lead-in responders); the paper's own conclusion calls for confirmation in larger trials.
This record does not independently assess randomization integrity, blinding adequacy, or missing-data handling beyond what the paper reports.
uncertainty_notes: This record qualifies the corpus's core question by addressing second-line augmentation of SSRI/SNRI treatment with a non-serotonergic adjunct (a kappa opioid receptor antagonist), rather than SSRI/SNRI monotherapy or head-to-head comparison. It should be read as evidence that not all augmentation strategies for SSRI/SNRI non-response are null -- unlike this corpus's agomelatine-augmentation record, aticaprant showed a significant benefit here.

source_title: Efficacy of empagliflozin as adjunctive therapy to citalopram in major depressive disorder: a randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?

intervention: Empagliflozin 10 mg daily, added to citalopram 40 mg daily.
comparator: Placebo, added to citalopram 40 mg daily.
outcome: Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) score at weeks 0, 4, and 8.
result_summary: HDRS scores in the placebo+citalopram group were 28.42 (SD 3.83), 20.20 (SD 3.82), and 13.42 (SD 3.42) at weeks 0, 4, and 8 respectively. In the empagliflozin+citalopram group, HDRS scores were 27.36 (SD 3.77), 13.76 (SD 1.40), and 7.00 (SD 1.13) at the same timepoints. Using repeated-measures ANOVA, the empagliflozin group showed significantly greater improvement in depression severity over time than the placebo group (p=0.0001).

source_title: The effect of escitalopram in treating mild to moderate depressive disorder and improving the quality of life in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting - a double-blind randomized clinical trial
research_question: Do selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) reduce depressive symptom severity in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD)?
claim_text: In a double-blind RCT in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) with comorbid mild-to-moderate depression, escitalopram significantly reduced depression scores and significantly improved quality of life compared to placebo.
population: 50 patients undergoing CABG at Tehran Heart Hospital (Jan-May 2021) with mild-to-moderate depression, randomly assigned to escitalopram or placebo.
intervention: Escitalopram, assessed at 4 and 8 weeks after treatment.
comparator: Placebo.
outcome: Depression severity via Beck's Depression Inventory; quality-of-life status and domains via the SF-36 questionnaire, at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks.
result_summary: No significant between-group difference existed at baseline in depression level (p=0.312) or quality of life (p=0.607). Escitalopram significantly reduced depression scores at weeks 4 and 8 compared to placebo (p<0.001). Quality of life and its domains were significantly higher in the escitalopram group at 8 weeks post-treatment compared to placebo.

source_span.locator_note: The baseline-comparability p-values and the week-4/week-8 depression and quality-of-life significance results this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: The most important effect of Escitalopram was reducing depression scores in the intervention group at weeks 4 and 8 after treatment compared to the placebo group (P<0.001). The quality of life and its domains were significantly higher in the Escitalopram group eight weeks after [treatment].
limitations: Small sample size (n=50 total, ~25 per arm) from a single center and a specific comorbid surgical population (post-CABG patients), not general-population MDD -- findings should not be generalized to first-line SSRI efficacy outside this context without caution.

This record's mild-to-moderate depression population differs from the moderate-to-severe MDD populations characterizing most of this corpus's other RCT records, limiting direct severity-matched comparison.

The abstract text available for this record reports significance (p-values) rather than raw per-group depression-score or SF-36 domain-score means, limiting the precision of this record's effect-size reporting.
This record does not independently assess randomization integrity, blinding adequacy, or missing-data handling beyond what the paper reports.

source_title: A retrospective analysis of combined treatment with escitalopram and Naoan dropping pills treatment for depression.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: A total of 87 patients

diagnosed with depression at The Third People’s Hospital of Tianshui over a 2-year period were retrospectively analyzed. Intervention: Group A (n = 43) received only escitalopram,

while group B (n = 44) received a combination of escitalopram and Naoan dropping pills for a period of 2 months. Comparator: This was quantified as <50% reduction

in the HAMD score compared to baseline, along with stag-

nant or unimproved hemodynamic indices. Outcome: Cerebral hemodynamics were

evaluated using transcranial Doppler ultrasound (TCD).
claim_text:
There were no statistical differences between

the 2 groups in terms of age, gender, education duration, BMI,

and disease course, between the group A and the group B

(P > .05).

research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Data were gathered from 180 subjects through a naturalistic

observation

study

of

trazodone

effectiveness

in

depression

(TED)

and

analyzed. Intervention: The TED study participants received trazodone XR of SSRIs in

ﬂexible doses for 12 weeks. Comparator: At baseline, the subjects treated with trazodone XR vs SSRIs presented

similar health status proﬁles and HRQoL values with respect to the mobility, self-

care, and anxiety/depression dimensions along with lower scores for the usual

activities, pain/discomfort, overall HRQoL, and health status. Outcome: The health status and health-related quality of life

(HRQoL) were evaluated using the EQ-5D-5L tool at baseline as well as 2, 4, 8,

and 12 weeks.
claim_text:
Compared to SSRIs, trazodone XR provided greater

improvements in terms of the self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and

anxiety/depression measures and more often improved participant overall health

status and HRQoL.

source_title: Prediction of depression treatment outcome from multimodal data: a CAN-BIND-1 report.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: In the CAN-BIND-1 dataset of 192 adults with MDD and outcomes of treatment

with escitalopram, we applied machine learning models in a nested cross-validation frame-

work. Intervention: The present study uses data from the first 8

weeks when all participants received escitalopram as a monother-

apy. Comparator: A combination of baseline tier 1 clinical, neuroimaging, and molecular variables pre-

dicted response with a mean balanced accuracy of 0.57 (best model mean 0.62) compared to

0.54 (best model mean 0.61) in single modality models. Outcome: Since we aimed to index improvement in a

way that is independent of baseline severity (Kennedy et al.,

2012), we chose response, defined as a reduction in MADRS by

50% or more from baseline to week 8, as the primary outcome

measure.
claim_text:
Using a single predictor modality led to

a mean accuracy of 0.542 (95% CI 0.541–0.543; S.E. = 0.000562),

the combination of two predictor modalities predicted a mean

accuracy of 0.553 (95% CI 0.552–0.554; S.E. = 0.000597), the com-

bination of features across all three modalities predicted response

with a mean balanced accuracy of 0.573 across methods (95% CI

0.571–0.575; S.E. = 0.000971).

within the tumor-containing region and tumor margin. Outcome: The primary classiﬁcation endpoint for model development was

objective response after ICI-chemotherapy.

limitations:
This study had some limitations. It was a retrospective single institution study, and

the cohort was small because PPC is rare. The cut-off values were determined by ROC

analysis using the same retrospective cohort and were not externally validated. Therefore,

these thresholds should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than

definitive and require validation in independent cohorts. Furthermore, the long period

of accrual spanning over two decades would inevitably have resulted in treatment being

heterogeneous, introducing potential confounding factors related to treatment-era effects.

Because multiple comparisons were performed without formal adjustment, the possibility

of false-positive findings cannot be excluded. In addition, we did not assess spatial immune

features or functional immune readouts. These limitations mean that our findings should

be interpreted cautiously and validated in larger multi-institutional cohorts.

limitations:
This study provides multifaceted

evidence, combining clinical outcome analyses with preclinical murine

research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Among 543 consecutively analyzed NSCLC cases, 93 patients harboring KRAS

mutations were identified and included in the final study cohort. Intervention: Study Design and Patient Selection

This retrospective single-center study included patients diagnosed with non-small

cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who underwent next-generation sequencing (NGS) analysis at

Ankara Atatürk Sanatoryum Training and Research Hospital between March 2024 and

March 2025. Comparator: Interestingly, STK11-mutated tumors demonstrated a trend toward lower PD-L1

expression levels and reduced frequency of high PD-L1 expression compared with STK11

https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm15135236 Outcome: Nucleic acid quantity and quality were

assessed using the Qubit 4 fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) to

determine suitability for sequencing analysis.
claim_text:
Among these, 93 patients (17.1%) harboring KRAS

mutations were identified and included in the study cohort.
population:
Among 543 consecutively analyzed NSCLC cases, 93 patients harboring KRAS

mutations were identified and included in the final study cohort.
intervention:
Study Design and Patient Selection

This retrospective single-center study included patients diagnosed with non-small

cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who underwent next-generation sequencing (NGS) analysis at

Ankara Atatürk Sanatoryum Training and Research Hospital between March 2024 and

March 2025.
comparator:
Interestingly, STK11-mutated tumors demonstrated a trend toward lower PD-L1

expression levels and reduced frequency of high PD-L1 expression compared with STK11

https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm15135236
outcome:
Nucleic acid quantity and quality were

assessed using the Qubit 4 fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) to

determine suitability for sequencing analysis.
result_summary:
Among these, 93 patients (17.1%) harboring KRAS

mutations were identified and included in the study cohort.
limitations:
Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the retrospective single-center

design may introduce inherent selection bias. Second, the relatively limited cohort size,

particularly within individual KRAS mutation subgroups and co-mutation categories, may

have limited the statistical power to detect modest prognostic associations. Therefore, the

absence of statistically significant differences should not be interpreted as evidence of a

true lack of biological or clinical relevance. Although our findings provide real-world data

from a well-characterized single-center cohort, they should be considered exploratory and

hypothesis-generating. Validation in larger multicenter cohorts and independent external

sequencing datasets is warranted to further clarify the prognostic significance of KRAS

molecular heterogeneity in NSCLC.

Furthermore, because detailed information regarding the exact timing of immunother-

apy initiation, treatment sequencing, ECOG performance status, and several other potential

confounding variables was not consistently available, advanced approaches such as time-

dependent Cox regression, landmark analyses, or propensity score adjustment could not

be performed. Therefore, the observed association between immunotherapy and overall

survival should be interpreted cautiously and considered hypothesis-generating.

As a retrospective single-center study, formal sensitivity analyses and a STROBE-style

participant flow diagram were not available.

The relatively short median follow-up duration may have limited the maturity and

reliability of the overall survival analyses. Therefore, the survival findings should be

interpreted with appropriate caution and require confirmation with longer follow-up

in future studies. PD-L1 expression was assessed using two clinically validated assays

(22C3 pharmDx and SP263). Although these assays are generally considered analytically

comparable, potential inter-assay variability cannot be completely excluded.

source_title: Fusion of Clinical and Deep Learning Features for Predicting Pembrolizumab Monotherapy Response in Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: All 114 patients underwent a baseline CT scan

6 weeks prior to treatment and a follow-up CT at 9–12 weeks after starting Pembrolizumab

therapy. Intervention: Materials: This study analyzed a retrospective cohort of NSCLC

patients treated with first-line PD-L1 monotherapy, divided into a discovery training set

(n: 97; 27 non-responders) and a preliminary test set (n: 17; 9 non-responders). Comparator: The VGG16 model was trained on group A: PR (40 patients, 564 ROIs) vs. PD

(27 patients, 563 ROIs). Outcome: Treat-

ment response was assessed using baseline and follow-up CT scans in accordance with

the response evaluation criteria in solid tumors (RECIST v1.1).
claim_text:
The model showed good

performance with five features: AUC of 0.72 ± 0.06 and F1 score of 0.45 on the discovery

set; AUC of 0.70 (95% CI: 0.403–0.957) and F1 score of 0.70 on the preliminary test set, as

shown in Figure 3a,b.

ment response was assessed using baseline and follow-up CT scans in accordance with

result_summary:
The model showed good

performance with five features: AUC of 0.72 ± 0.06 and F1 score of 0.45 on the discovery

set; AUC of 0.70 (95% CI: 0.403–0.957) and F1 score of 0.70 on the preliminary test set, as

shown in Figure 3a,b.
limitations:
While previous DL-based immunotherapy studies have shown that DL features com-

plement clinical, genomic, and metastasis variables, and that selective DL feature subsets

can improve model stability, these approaches have several limitations [14–22].
However, several limitations exist.

A limitation of

this study is that a simple equal-weight averaging strategy was used for multimodal fusion.

To address additional limitations of this study, future work will propose three key

directions.

source_title: Inflammatory biomarkers refine progression risk stratification in NSCLC patients with stable disease.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Patients’ characteristics and treatment response

A total of 179 patients treated in a palliative setting for advanced

NSCLC with available imaging between January 2019 and December

2024 were screened. Intervention: All

included patients were ≥18 years of age, had histologically confirmed

NSCLC of locally advanced or metastatic stage and received intravenous

systemic anti-neoplastic treatment regimen in a palliative intend. Comparator: The combined clinical-inflammatory model showed the highest apparent discriminative

performance (AUC 0.766), compared to clinical-only (AUC 0.657) and inflammatory-only models (AUC 0.727),

although the incremental improvement was modest. Outcome: This endpoint is conditional on patients remaining

progression-free and alive long enough to meet this definition and was

therefore used to discriminate outcomes within the subgroup of patients

with stable disease at first restaging rather than to model long-term

survival.

source_title: Inflammatory biomarkers refine progression risk stratification in NSCLC patients with stable disease.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Patients’ characteristics and treatment response

A total of 179 patients treated in a palliative setting for advanced

NSCLC with available imaging between January 2019 and December

2024 were screened. Intervention: All

included patients were ≥18 years of age, had histologically confirmed

NSCLC of locally advanced or metastatic stage and received intravenous

systemic anti-neoplastic treatment regimen in a palliative intend. Comparator: The combined clinical-inflammatory model showed the highest apparent discriminative

performance (AUC 0.766), compared to clinical-only (AUC 0.657) and inflammatory-only models (AUC 0.727),

although the incremental improvement was modest. Outcome: This endpoint is conditional on patients remaining

progression-free and alive long enough to meet this definition and was

therefore used to discriminate outcomes within the subgroup of patients

with stable disease at first restaging rather than to model long-term

survival.
claim_text:
Regarding systemic antineoplastic therapy,

chemo-immunotherapy was used in 39 patients (49%), immunotherapy

alone in 27 (34%) and chemotherapy in 13 (16%) - one patient received

chemotherapy plus targeted therapy.

source_title: Clinical Value of the Systemic Immune Inflammation Index and PD-L1 Expression in Advanced NSCLC Treated with Pembrolizumab: Real-World Preliminary Study.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Results: A total of 102 patients were included. Intervention: 2.1 Study Design and Patients

We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with NSCLC who received pembrolizumab in

various clinical settings at INHA university hospital between 2017 and March 2024. Comparator: These findings indicate that lower pretreatment SII values were significantly

associated with longer PFS and OS in patients treated with pembrolizumab compared to patients with high

SII values. Outcome: The impact of each clinical factor on survival outcomes

was assessed using the Kaplan–Meier method, and comparisons were made using the log-rank test for

univariate analysis.
claim_text:

associated with longer PFS and OS in patients treated with pembrolizumab compared to patients with high

SII values.

result_summary:
These findings indicate that lower pretreatment SII values were significantly

associated with longer PFS and OS in patients treated with pembrolizumab compared to patients with high

SII values.
limitations:
These findings

imply that the SII may complement the limitations of PD-L1 as a standalone predictive biomarker for

immunotherapy response.

The limitations of PD-L1 expression as a standalone biomarker may be addressed by combining it

with inflammatory parameters.

These findings support the hypothesis that CBC-IBs can compensate

for the limitations of PD-L1 alone in identifying patients more likely to benefit from immunotherapy.
As a single-center real-world preliminary study, our study has several limitations.

To mitigate these limitations

and enhance the robustness of our analysis, we prospectively performed validated PD-L1 IHC analysis

on diagnostic tumor samples for all included patients.

research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Results: A total of 102 patients were included. Intervention: 2.1 Study Design and Patients

We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with NSCLC who received pembrolizumab in

various clinical settings at INHA university hospital between 2017 and March 2024. Comparator: These findings indicate that lower pretreatment SII values were significantly

associated with longer PFS and OS in patients treated with pembrolizumab compared to patients with high

SII values. Outcome: The impact of each clinical factor on survival outcomes

was assessed using the Kaplan–Meier method, and comparisons were made using the log-rank test for

univariate analysis.
claim_text:
In particular, the MST was 22 months in group A versus 12 months in group B (p = 0.002),

whereas the median PFS was 13 months versus 5 months, respectively (p = 0.026; Fig. 3).
population: Results: A total of 102 patients were included.
intervention:

outcome:

result_summary:
In particular, the MST was 22 months in group A versus 12 months in group B (p = 0.002),

whereas the median PFS was 13 months versus 5 months, respectively (p = 0.026; Fig. 3).
limitations:
These findings

imply that the SII may complement the limitations of PD-L1 as a standalone predictive biomarker for

immunotherapy response.

The limitations of PD-L1 expression as a standalone biomarker may be addressed by combining it

with inflammatory parameters.

These findings support the hypothesis that CBC-IBs can compensate

for the limitations of PD-L1 alone in identifying patients more likely to benefit from immunotherapy.
As a single-center real-world preliminary study, our study has several limitations.

To mitigate these limitations

and enhance the robustness of our analysis, we prospectively performed validated PD-L1 IHC analysis

on diagnostic tumor samples for all included patients.

In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Results: Among

452 patients, 151 (33.4%) experienced irAEs of any grade, and 37 (8.2%) developed grade

≥3 events. Intervention: Methods: We conducted a multicenter,

retrospective study including patients with advanced NSCLC treated with ICIs alone or in

combination with chemotherapy between April 2017 and December 2023. Comparator: Categorical variables were analyzed using chi-square tests, while PFS and OS were

estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method and compared with the log-rank test. Outcome: Efficacy was evaluated using objective response rate (ORR), progression-free survival (PFS),

and overall survival (OS).
claim_text:
Patients with ≥2 irAE episodes (n = 36) had longer PFS than those without irAEs

(46.3 vs. 4.2 months; HR = 0.24; 95% CI: 0.16–0.35; p < 0.001), and a single irAE episode

(n = 112) was also associated with prolonged PFS compared to the no-irAE group (21.1 vs.

4.2 months; HR = 0.38; 95% CI: 0.29–0.51; p < 0.001).

research_question:

treatment blood was drawn on the same day prior to the ﬁrst

administration of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor for 113 patients (57

patients aged over 70 was recorded in the cohort B (51.8%)

reliability in risk stratiﬁcation.

In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: A total of 34 studies involving 1,885 patients were included. Intervention: It is crucial to provide context for this estimate: it applies

neoadjuvant therapy and subsequently underwent resection. Comparator: Our results provide

preliminary evidence and rationale for initiating randomized controlled clinical

trials in this population to compare the efﬁcacy and safety of surgery after

neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy versus current standard therapy. Outcome: Quality assessment

The 34 studies were evaluated using the JBI Critical Appraisal

Checklist for Case Series (48).

surgical resection rate was 76.0% (95% CI: 70.0%−82.0%; I2 = 89.34%).

The 34 studies were evaluated using the JBI Critical Appraisal

Checklist for Case Series (48).
result_summary:
The pooled

surgical resection rate was 76.0% (95% CI: 70.0%−82.0%; I2 = 89.34%).
limitations:
This meta-analysis has several important limitations that warrant

consideration when interpreting the ﬁndings. First, the predominance

of single-arm trials and small cohort studies—without inclusion of

randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or phase III trials—introduces

potential biases in key outcome measures such as surgical

complication rates, R0 resection rates, and surgical resectability

metrics. The lack of comparative data from RCTs makes it difﬁcult

to draw deﬁnitive conclusions about the relative feasibility of

neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy compared to standard treat-

ments like the PACIFIC regimen (concurrent chemoradiotherapy

followed by durvalumab maintenance).

Second, the immature long-term survival data currently available

preclude robust evaluation of whether the observed improvements in

pathological responses (pCR/mPR) translate into meaningful PFS or

OS beneﬁts. While pathological response rates are promising surro-

gate endpoints, their correlation with long-term survival outcomes

remains to be fully validated in this patient population.

Third, the complexity of surgical interventions following

neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy may elevate perioperative

risks, necessitating involvement of highly experienced thoracic

surgeons. The observed surgical complication rate of 6% (95% CI:

0.03–0.09) may underestimate real-world risks, as the included

studies were predominantly conducted at high-volume centers

with specialized surgical expertise.

Fourth, the deﬁnition of “potentially resectable” status exhibits

subjectivity dependent on MDT assessment and institutional prac-

tices. The inclusion of heterogeneous patient populations—particu-

larly those with N2/N3 lymph node involvement or T3–4 tumors—

raises unresolved questions about the generalizability of R0 resection

rates and survival outcomes across different clinical scenarios.

10

To mitigate these concerns, we implemented rigorous statistical

methods including subgroup analyses and publication bias correc-

tion (Egger’s test + trim-and-ﬁll method). However, the substantial

between-study heterogeneity (I2 > 50% for most outcomes) and

small sample sizes in many included studies (total n = 1,885)

warrant cautious interpretation of the pooled estimates. The trim-

and-ﬁll analysis revealed signiﬁcant publication bias for R0 resec-

tion rates and surgical complications, suggesting that the reported

effect sizes may overestimate true treatment effects. These limita-

tions highlight the need for larger, RCTs with standardized deﬁni-

tions of resectability and longer follow-up to validate these

preliminary ﬁndings.

source_title: Feasibility of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy in potentially resectable non-small cell lung cancer: a single-arm meta-analysis.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: A total of 34 studies involving 1,885 patients were included. Intervention: It is crucial to provide context for this estimate: it applies

only to the subset of patients who successfully completed

neoadjuvant therapy and subsequently underwent resection. Comparator: Our results provide

preliminary evidence and rationale for initiating randomized controlled clinical

trials in this population to compare the efﬁcacy and safety of surgery after

neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy versus current standard therapy. Outcome: Quality assessment

The 34 studies were evaluated using the JBI Critical Appraisal

Checklist for Case Series (48).

CI: 0.21–0.29), as shown in Figure 2D.

limitations:
This meta-analysis has several important limitations that warrant

consideration when interpreting the ﬁndings. First, the predominance

of single-arm trials and small cohort studies—without inclusion of

randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or phase III trials—introduces

potential biases in key outcome measures such as surgical

complication rates, R0 resection rates, and surgical resectability

metrics. The lack of comparative data from RCTs makes it difﬁcult

to draw deﬁnitive conclusions about the relative feasibility of

neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy compared to standard treat-

ments like the PACIFIC regimen (concurrent chemoradiotherapy

followed by durvalumab maintenance).

Second, the immature long-term survival data currently available

preclude robust evaluation of whether the observed improvements in

pathological responses (pCR/mPR) translate into meaningful PFS or

OS beneﬁts. While pathological response rates are promising surro-

gate endpoints, their correlation with long-term survival outcomes

remains to be fully validated in this patient population.

Third, the complexity of surgical interventions following

neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy may elevate perioperative

risks, necessitating involvement of highly experienced thoracic

surgeons. The observed surgical complication rate of 6% (95% CI:

0.03–0.09) may underestimate real-world risks, as the included

studies were predominantly conducted at high-volume centers

with specialized surgical expertise.

Fourth, the deﬁnition of “potentially resectable” status exhibits

subjectivity dependent on MDT assessment and institutional prac-

tices. The inclusion of heterogeneous patient populations—particu-

larly those with N2/N3 lymph node involvement or T3–4 tumors—

raises unresolved questions about the generalizability of R0 resection

rates and survival outcomes across different clinical scenarios.

Wu et al.

Frontiers in Oncology

10

To mitigate these concerns, we implemented rigorous statistical

methods including subgroup analyses and publication bias correc-

tion (Egger’s test + trim-and-ﬁll method). However, the substantial

between-study heterogeneity (I2 > 50% for most outcomes) and

small sample sizes in many included studies (total n = 1,885)

warrant cautious interpretation of the pooled estimates. The trim-

and-ﬁll analysis revealed signiﬁcant publication bias for R0 resec-

tion rates and surgical complications, suggesting that the reported

effect sizes may overestimate true treatment effects. These limita-

tions highlight the need for larger, RCTs with standardized deﬁni-

tions of resectability and longer follow-up to validate these

preliminary ﬁndings.

research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Results We first validated across three independent cohorts of 589 patients with melanoma or NSCLC treated

with ICI that grade ≥ 2 irAE were associated with significantly longer overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival

(PFS). Intervention: Among them, 29 patients (28%)

received combined ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) and

nivolumab (anti-PD-1) treatment. Comparator: Complementary analysis using shotgun metagenomics and culturomics revealed that patients who developed

assessed using principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) based on Bray–Curtis dissimilarity, and ellipses indicate the 95% confidence interval of group

centroids.

total of 125 patients were included, of whom 73 received pembrolizumab and 52 received

atezolizumab. Intervention: Patients were treated with

limitations:
This study has several limitations. First, its retrospective, single-center design is

subject to inherent biases, including incomplete data capture and unmeasured confounding.

Although data were retrieved from electronic health records, variability in documentation

and follow-up cannot be excluded. We acknowledge that immune-related adverse events

were analyzed as a time-fixed variable (yes/no), and time-dependent modeling was not

feasible due to non-standardized retrospective recording of irAE onset dates; therefore,

potential immortal-time bias cannot be fully excluded.

Second, the relatively small sample size limits statistical power, particularly for sub-

group analyses, and may have reduced the ability to detect modest differences between

atezolizumab and pembrolizumab. (e.g., PD-L1 strata further split by treatment arm)

Third, molecular testing during the study period was limited primarily to EGFR and

ALK alterations, as comprehensive genomic profiling was not routinely available, which

may have resulted in incomplete exclusion of rare oncogenic drivers. In addition, at the

time of analysis, overall survival data were immature due to the relatively short follow-up

after the introduction of atezolizumab, and therefore, progression-free survival was used

as the primary endpoint. While PFS is a clinically meaningful outcome in this setting,

longer follow-up will be required to assess overall survival and confirm the durability of

treatment benefit.

Additionally, PD-L1 tumor proportion score and age were analyzed as dichotomized

variables despite being continuous by nature, which may have led to loss of informa-

tion and limited the ability to detect more subtle associations with outcomes. Age was

dichotomized using a clinically relevant threshold (≥70 years), consistent with prior real-

world immunotherapy studies in elderly NSCLC populations. PD-L1 TPS was categorized

as 50–89% versus ≥90% based on previous reports suggesting differential outcomes among

patients with very high PD-L1 expression. Moreover, the numerically higher proportion

of patients with ECOG PS 2 and the lower proportion of patients with very high PD-L1

expression (TPS ≥90%) in the pembrolizumab group may represent a potential source of

residual confounding. Although multivariable adjustment was performed, unmeasured or

incompletely captured factors may have influenced outcomes. The absence of statistical

significance should not be interpreted as proof of equivalence. Given sample size and

https://doi.org/10.3390/cancers18071153

11 of 13

event numbers, the study may be underpowered to detect modest differences; therefore,

findings should be interpreted as suggesting comparable effectiveness within the limits of

observational data and available follow-up.

Finally, as a real-world study from a single academic center in a resource-limited

setting, treatment patterns, patient characteristics, and access to diagnostics may differ from

those in other healthcare systems, potentially limiting the generalizability of the findings.

Despite these limitations, this study reflects routine clinical practice following the

introduction of atezolizumab for this indication and provides clinically relevant real-world

evidence comparing atezolizumab and pembrolizumab monotherapy in patients with high

PD-L1-expressing metastatic NSCLC.

research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Results: A total of 302 patients were included in the

analysis. Intervention: A total of 302 patients with extensive-stage SCLC received

the combination of atezolizumab with carboplatin and etoposide between 1 January 2022

and 31 December 2024. Comparator: The real-world progression-free survival (PFS) in our study surpassed that in

IMpower133 (7.6 versus 5.2 months), in addition to higher PFS rates beyond six months. Outcome: Survival Analysis

Survival outcomes were visualized via Kaplan–Meier curves, with confidence intervals

calculated using Greenwood’s method, and differences between the real-world cohort

and the Impower133 trial were assessed using the log-rank test.

analysis. Intervention: A total of 302 patients with extensive-stage SCLC received

and 31 December 2024. Comparator: The real-world progression-free survival (PFS) in our study surpassed that in

IMpower133 (7.6 versus 5.2 months), in addition to higher PFS rates beyond six months. Outcome: Survival Analysis

calculated using Greenwood’s method, and differences between the real-world cohort

and the Impower133 trial were assessed using the log-rank test.

analysis. Intervention: A total of 302 patients with extensive-stage SCLC received

the combination of atezolizumab with carboplatin and etoposide between 1 January 2022

and 31 December 2024. Comparator: The real-world progression-free survival (PFS) in our study surpassed that in

IMpower133 (7.6 versus 5.2 months), in addition to higher PFS rates beyond six months. Outcome: Survival Analysis

Survival outcomes were visualized via Kaplan–Meier curves, with confidence intervals

calculated using Greenwood’s method, and differences between the real-world cohort

and the Impower133 trial were assessed using the log-rank test.
claim_text:

(95% CI 74.6–89.3, n = 92) versus 88.1% (95% CI 82.5–92.4, n = 163), with no statistically

significant difference between groups (chi-square p = 0.207).

source_title: Addition of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor to Platinum Retreatment for Recurrent Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer After Perioperative Chemotherapy: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Among 124 patients who received perioperative platinum therapy and surgery, 31 underwent platinum retreatment: 17

in the chemo group and 14 in the ICI-­chemo group. Intervention: Patients were categorized into either the “chemo group,” who received platinum retreatment without ICI, or the “ICI-­chemo

group,” who received platinum retreatment with ICI. Comparator: The KEYNOTE-­189 study, which evaluated the efficacy of add­

ing ICI to platinum therapy in advanced NSCLC, reported a sig­

nificant increase in both PFS and OS in the intention-­to-­treat

population (median PFS 9.0 vs. 4.9 months, HR 0.50; median OS

22.0 vs. 10.6 months, HR 0.60) [13]. Outcome: The primary endpoint was progression-­free survival in patients treated

with ICI.
claim_text:
PFS was significantly longer in the ICI-­chemo group than in the chemo group

(15.4 vs. 5.9 months; log-­rank p = 0.023; HR 0.40, 95% CI, 0.18–0.90).

were identified from 132 patients treated with RT/CT + IO at a comprehensive cancer

center. Intervention: Methods:

of infiltrate and dose per bin compared with a linear–quadratic dose–response model

Criterion (AIC). Outcome: The primary endpoint of the study

was the analysis of the existence of a dose–response relationship.

source_title: Comparison of 6 cycles with 4 cycles of chemotherapy and atezolizumab in the first-line treatment of ES-SCLC: a retrospective multicenter analysis.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: A total of 181 patients

with ES-SCLC who received first-line treatment with chemotherapy plus atezolizumab were analyzed and grouped into

those receiving 4 cycles (n = 101) and 6 cycles (n = 80) of treatment. Intervention: A total of

194 patients with ES-SCLC (n = 194) treated with carbo/etop plus

atezolizumab between January 2019 and November 2024 were

identified from medical records. Comparator: This is one of the largest real-world datasets comparing the efficacy and safety of 4 versus 6 cycles of

induction chemoimmunotherapy. Outcome: Therefore, PFS should be inter­

preted as a time-to-event outcome reflecting real-world clinical

decision-making, rather than a strictly standardized endpoint com­

parable to that of prospective clinical trials.
claim_text:
The objective response rates were similar between the 4- and 6-cycle groups

(79.2% vs 78.8%, P=.940).
population:
A total of 181 patients

with ES-SCLC who received first-line treatment with chemotherapy plus atezolizumab were analyzed and grouped into

those receiving 4 cycles (n = 101) and 6 cycles (n = 80) of treatment.
intervention:
A total of

194 patients with ES-SCLC (n = 194) treated with carbo/etop plus

atezolizumab between January 2019 and November 2024 were

identified from medical records.
comparator:
This is one of the largest real-world datasets comparing the efficacy and safety of 4 versus 6 cycles of

induction chemoimmunotherapy.
outcome:
Therefore, PFS should be inter­

preted as a time-to-event outcome reflecting real-world clinical

decision-making, rather than a strictly standardized endpoint com­

parable to that of prospective clinical trials.
result_summary:
The objective response rates were similar between the 4- and 6-cycle groups

(79.2% vs 78.8%, P=.940).
limitations:
In patients receiving PD-1

and PD-L1 blockage, the presence of irAEs was associated with

improved PFS and OS in the advanced stages of non-small-cell

lung cancer, gastric cancer, urothelial carcinoma, and head and

neck cancer.30 However, in a Japanese cohort of 40 patients

with ES-SCLC, the presence of irAEs was not associated with sur­

vival outcomes study.31

The major limitation of our study is its retrospective design.

As a result of the retrospective data collection, the detailed

chemotherapy toxicity profile of the study population and the

progression sites for 23 of 142 patients who had disease pro­

gression (16.2%) were missing, which may represent a limitation

of our analysis.

Another limitation of our study is that our data

did not include PFS-2 analysis.

source_title: Comparison of 6 cycles with 4 cycles of chemotherapy and atezolizumab in the first-line treatment of ES-SCLC: a retrospective multicenter analysis.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: A total of 181 patients

with ES-SCLC who received first-line treatment with chemotherapy plus atezolizumab were analyzed and grouped into

those receiving 4 cycles (n = 101) and 6 cycles (n = 80) of treatment. Intervention: A total of

194 patients with ES-SCLC (n = 194) treated with carbo/etop plus

atezolizumab between January 2019 and November 2024 were

identified from medical records. Comparator: This is one of the largest real-world datasets comparing the efficacy and safety of 4 versus 6 cycles of

induction chemoimmunotherapy. Outcome: Therefore, PFS should be inter­

preted as a time-to-event outcome reflecting real-world clinical

decision-making, rather than a strictly standardized endpoint com­

parable to that of prospective clinical trials.
claim_text:
Conclusion: This is one of the largest real-world datasets comparing the efficacy and safety of 4 versus 6 cycles of

induction chemoimmunotherapy.
population:
A total of 181 patients

with ES-SCLC who received first-line treatment with chemotherapy plus atezolizumab were analyzed and grouped into

those receiving 4 cycles (n = 101) and 6 cycles (n = 80) of treatment.
intervention:
A total of

194 patients with ES-SCLC (n = 194) treated with carbo/etop plus

atezolizumab between January 2019 and November 2024 were

identified from medical records.
comparator:
This is one of the largest real-world datasets comparing the efficacy and safety of 4 versus 6 cycles of

induction chemoimmunotherapy.
outcome:
Therefore, PFS should be inter­

preted as a time-to-event outcome reflecting real-world clinical

decision-making, rather than a strictly standardized endpoint com­

parable to that of prospective clinical trials.
result_summary:
Conclusion: This is one of the largest real-world datasets comparing the efficacy and safety of 4 versus 6 cycles of

induction chemoimmunotherapy.
limitations:
In patients receiving PD-1

and PD-L1 blockage, the presence of irAEs was associated with

improved PFS and OS in the advanced stages of non-small-cell

lung cancer, gastric cancer, urothelial carcinoma, and head and

neck cancer.30 However, in a Japanese cohort of 40 patients

with ES-SCLC, the presence of irAEs was not associated with sur­

vival outcomes study.31

The major limitation of our study is its retrospective design.

As a result of the retrospective data collection, the detailed

chemotherapy toxicity profile of the study population and the

progression sites for 23 of 142 patients who had disease pro­

gression (16.2%) were missing, which may represent a limitation

of our analysis.

Another limitation of our study is that our data

did not include PFS-2 analysis.

source_title: Comparison of 6 cycles with 4 cycles of chemotherapy and atezolizumab in the first-line treatment of ES-SCLC: a retrospective multicenter analysis.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: A total of 181 patients

with ES-SCLC who received first-line treatment with chemotherapy plus atezolizumab were analyzed and grouped into

those receiving 4 cycles (n = 101) and 6 cycles (n = 80) of treatment. Intervention: A total of

194 patients with ES-SCLC (n = 194) treated with carbo/etop plus

atezolizumab between January 2019 and November 2024 were

identified from medical records. Comparator: This is one of the largest real-world datasets comparing the efficacy and safety of 4 versus 6 cycles of

induction chemoimmunotherapy. Outcome: Therefore, PFS should be inter­

preted as a time-to-event outcome reflecting real-world clinical

decision-making, rather than a strictly standardized endpoint com­

parable to that of prospective clinical trials.
claim_text:
The liver progression event ratio in

patients without baseline liver metastasis was 27.9% (12 of the

43 patients).
population:
A total of 181 patients

with ES-SCLC who received first-line treatment with chemotherapy plus atezolizumab were analyzed and grouped into

those receiving 4 cycles (n = 101) and 6 cycles (n = 80) of treatment.
intervention:
A total of

194 patients with ES-SCLC (n = 194) treated with carbo/etop plus

atezolizumab between January 2019 and November 2024 were

identified from medical records.
comparator:
This is one of the largest real-world datasets comparing the efficacy and safety of 4 versus 6 cycles of

induction chemoimmunotherapy.
outcome:
Therefore, PFS should be inter­

preted as a time-to-event outcome reflecting real-world clinical

decision-making, rather than a strictly standardized endpoint com­

parable to that of prospective clinical trials.
result_summary:
The liver progression event ratio in

patients without baseline liver metastasis was 27.9% (12 of the

43 patients).
limitations:
In patients receiving PD-1

and PD-L1 blockage, the presence of irAEs was associated with

improved PFS and OS in the advanced stages of non-small-cell

lung cancer, gastric cancer, urothelial carcinoma, and head and

neck cancer.30 However, in a Japanese cohort of 40 patients

with ES-SCLC, the presence of irAEs was not associated with sur­

vival outcomes study.31

The major limitation of our study is its retrospective design.

As a result of the retrospective data collection, the detailed

chemotherapy toxicity profile of the study population and the

progression sites for 23 of 142 patients who had disease pro­

gression (16.2%) were missing, which may represent a limitation

of our analysis.

Another limitation of our study is that our data

did not include PFS-2 analysis.

Outcome measures: Efficacy assessment: Tumor response

was evaluated according to the criteria established by the

Union for International Cancer Control and the WHO.9

Treatment responses were categorized as follows:

•

Complete response (CR): Disappearance of all tumor

lesions sustained for at least one month;

•

Partial response (PR): ≥50% reduction in tumor

burden without disease progression, sustained for at

least one month, with no new lesions;

•

Stable disease (SD): <50% reduction or ≤25% increase

in tumor burden, sustained for at least one month;

Progressive disease (PD): >25% increase in tumor

burden or the appearance of new lesions.

research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: Patients and Treatments

A total of 217 patients were included in this study (Figure 1). Intervention: Patients di-

agnosed between January 2019 and December 2023 with advanced PD-L1 <1% NSCLC

and treated with palliative intent at IUCPQ were included and categorized by first-line

treatment. Comparator: For OS and PFS,

Kaplan–Meier survival curves were generated for the CT + IO and CT groups, and an

exploratory subgroup analysis was conducted based on histological subtype (squamous

vs. nonsquamous). Outcome: Prognostic factors were evaluated using Cox regression.
claim_text:
Eighty-two (37.8%)

were treated with CT + IO, 32 (14.7%) with CT alone, 16 (7.4%) with targeted therapies

and 87 (40.1%) with supportive care.
