source_title: Baseline glucose-to-lymphocyte ratio predicts nivolumab outcomes in advanced non-small cell lung cancer: a multicenter retrospective study.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: We retrospectively analyzed 837 patients with advanced or metastatic

NSCLC treated with nivolumab across 21 oncology centers in Turkey (2015–

2025). Intervention: Patients with advanced or

metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who received

nivolumab between January 2015 and January 2025 were

included. Comparator: Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS)

were estimated using Kaplan–Meier and compared with log-rank tests. Outcome: Clinical outcomes

The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS),

deﬁned as the time from nivolumab initiation to the ﬁrst

documented disease progression or death from any cause.
claim_text:
Results: The optimal GLR cut-off for mortality was ≥70.76 (AUC = 0.635, 95% CI:

0.597–0.674; p < 0.001).
population:
We retrospectively analyzed 837 patients with advanced or metastatic

NSCLC treated with nivolumab across 21 oncology centers in Turkey (2015–

2025).
intervention:
Patients with advanced or

metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who received

nivolumab between January 2015 and January 2025 were

included.
comparator:
Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS)

were estimated using Kaplan–Meier and compared with log-rank tests.
outcome:
Clinical outcomes

The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS),

deﬁned as the time from nivolumab initiation to the ﬁrst

documented disease progression or death from any cause.
result_summary:
Results: The optimal GLR cut-off for mortality was ≥70.76 (AUC = 0.635, 95% CI:

0.597–0.674; p < 0.001).
limitations:
This study has several limitations. First, its retrospective

multicenter design introduces risks of selection bias and

heterogeneity in clinical practice patterns across centers. Second,

GLR was measured only at baseline, and dynamic on-treatment

changes—which may offer additional prognostic or predictive

insights for immunotherapy—could not be assessed due to the

retrospective nature of data collection. Third, molecular correlates

such as tumor mutational burden, T-cell clonality, or tumor

microenvironmental characteristics were not available, limiting

our ability to mechanistically validate the observed associations.

In addition, incomplete availability of established biomarkers—

particularly PD-L1 expression and tumor mutational burden—

precluded direct comparative or integrative analyses, limiting

deﬁnitive conclusions regarding the incremental therapeutic

utility of GLR relative to tumor-based or inﬂammation-

derived biomarkers.

Another important limitation is the absence of an external

validation cohort. Although the dataset included patients from 21

institutions, all centers contributed through a uniﬁed national

electronic registry, which prevented the formation of an

independent validation subset. Thus, while the prognostic effect of

GLR remained directionally consistent across multiple clinically

relevant subgroups, external validation in independent populations

is required before clinical implementation. Furthermore, patients in

the high-GLR group more frequently exhibited poorer ECOG

performance status at baseline. Although ECOG was adjusted for

in multivariate analyses, residual confounding related to baseline

functional status cannot be entirely excluded.

Moreover, because GLR incorporates fasting glucose, non–

tumor-related factors—including diabetes mellitus, corticosteroid

exposure, metabolic syndrome, or acute inﬂammation—may

inﬂuence its value. Baseline corticosteroid use was not uniformly

documented across participating centers and therefore could not be

reliably included in multivariate analyses, representing an inherent

limitation of this retrospective real-world dataset. Detailed

metabolic parameters (e.g., HbA1c) and comprehensive

medication histories were not uniformly available across centers,

limiting our ability to adjust for these confounders and representing

an inherent constraint of retrospective real-world datasets.

Similarly, detailed nivolumab exposure data, including exact cycle

numbers, were not consistently recorded across all participating

centers, precluding a reliable cycle-based exposure analysis for the

entire cohort.

Finally, variability in imaging schedules and follow-up intervals

across institutions may have introduced measurement noise,

particularly affecting PFS assessments, despite adherence to

national nivolumab monitoring guidelines. Future prospective

studies with harmonized imaging protocols, standardized

metabolic assessments, and longitudinal GLR measurements—as

survival (OS). ECOG performance status and GLR ≥70.76 were

independent predictors of worse OS, whereas prior thoracic

radiotherapy was associated with improved OS. Hazard ratios (HRs)

are presented with 95% conﬁdence intervals (CIs).

Ersoy et al.

well as multicenter registries speciﬁcally designed for biomarker

validation incorporating external validation cohorts, resampling

techniques (e.g., bootstrapping), and calibration analyses—will be

essential to conﬁrm the reproducibility and generalizability of GLR

as a prognostic biomarker.

Clinical implications

GLR is inexpensive, reproducible, and universally available.

Unlike PD-L1 expression or tumor mutational burden, it requires

no specialized testing and can be obtained repeatedly from routine

blood work. GLR may therefore serve as a practical stratiﬁcation

tool, identifying high-risk patients who warrant closer monitoring,

alternative systemic strategies, or enrollment in clinical trials of

novel combinations.

source_title: Baseline glucose-to-lymphocyte ratio predicts nivolumab outcomes in advanced non-small cell lung cancer: a multicenter retrospective study.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: We retrospectively analyzed 837 patients with advanced or metastatic

NSCLC treated with nivolumab across 21 oncology centers in Turkey (2015–

2025). Intervention: Patients with advanced or

metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who received

nivolumab between January 2015 and January 2025 were

included. Comparator: Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS)

were estimated using Kaplan–Meier and compared with log-rank tests. Outcome: Clinical outcomes

The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS),

deﬁned as the time from nivolumab initiation to the ﬁrst

documented disease progression or death from any cause.
claim_text:
Patients with GLR <70.76 achieved signiﬁcantly

longer OS compared with those with GLR ≥70.76 (median 24.1 vs 9.6

months; log-rank p < 0.001; Figure 2A).

intervention:

comparator:
Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS)

Clinical outcomes

The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS),

result_summary:
Patients with GLR <70.76 achieved signiﬁcantly

longer OS compared with those with GLR ≥70.76 (median 24.1 vs 9.6

months; log-rank p < 0.001; Figure 2A).
limitations:
This study has several limitations. First, its retrospective

multicenter design introduces risks of selection bias and

heterogeneity in clinical practice patterns across centers. Second,

GLR was measured only at baseline, and dynamic on-treatment

changes—which may offer additional prognostic or predictive

insights for immunotherapy—could not be assessed due to the

retrospective nature of data collection. Third, molecular correlates

such as tumor mutational burden, T-cell clonality, or tumor

microenvironmental characteristics were not available, limiting

our ability to mechanistically validate the observed associations.

In addition, incomplete availability of established biomarkers—

particularly PD-L1 expression and tumor mutational burden—

precluded direct comparative or integrative analyses, limiting

deﬁnitive conclusions regarding the incremental therapeutic

utility of GLR relative to tumor-based or inﬂammation-

derived biomarkers.

Another important limitation is the absence of an external

validation cohort. Although the dataset included patients from 21

institutions, all centers contributed through a uniﬁed national

electronic registry, which prevented the formation of an

independent validation subset. Thus, while the prognostic effect of

GLR remained directionally consistent across multiple clinically

relevant subgroups, external validation in independent populations

is required before clinical implementation. Furthermore, patients in

the high-GLR group more frequently exhibited poorer ECOG

performance status at baseline. Although ECOG was adjusted for

in multivariate analyses, residual confounding related to baseline

functional status cannot be entirely excluded.

Moreover, because GLR incorporates fasting glucose, non–

tumor-related factors—including diabetes mellitus, corticosteroid

exposure, metabolic syndrome, or acute inﬂammation—may

inﬂuence its value. Baseline corticosteroid use was not uniformly

documented across participating centers and therefore could not be

reliably included in multivariate analyses, representing an inherent

limitation of this retrospective real-world dataset. Detailed

metabolic parameters (e.g., HbA1c) and comprehensive

medication histories were not uniformly available across centers,

limiting our ability to adjust for these confounders and representing

an inherent constraint of retrospective real-world datasets.

Similarly, detailed nivolumab exposure data, including exact cycle

numbers, were not consistently recorded across all participating

centers, precluding a reliable cycle-based exposure analysis for the

entire cohort.

Finally, variability in imaging schedules and follow-up intervals

across institutions may have introduced measurement noise,

particularly affecting PFS assessments, despite adherence to

national nivolumab monitoring guidelines. Future prospective

studies with harmonized imaging protocols, standardized

metabolic assessments, and longitudinal GLR measurements—as

survival (OS). ECOG performance status and GLR ≥70.76 were

independent predictors of worse OS, whereas prior thoracic

radiotherapy was associated with improved OS. Hazard ratios (HRs)

are presented with 95% conﬁdence intervals (CIs).

Ersoy et al.

well as multicenter registries speciﬁcally designed for biomarker

validation incorporating external validation cohorts, resampling

techniques (e.g., bootstrapping), and calibration analyses—will be

essential to conﬁrm the reproducibility and generalizability of GLR

as a prognostic biomarker.

Clinical implications

GLR is inexpensive, reproducible, and universally available.

Unlike PD-L1 expression or tumor mutational burden, it requires

no specialized testing and can be obtained repeatedly from routine

blood work. GLR may therefore serve as a practical stratiﬁcation

tool, identifying high-risk patients who warrant closer monitoring,

alternative systemic strategies, or enrollment in clinical trials of

novel combinations.

source_title: Baseline glucose-to-lymphocyte ratio predicts nivolumab outcomes in advanced non-small cell lung cancer: a multicenter retrospective study.
research_question:
In the following population, does the intervention affect the outcome, compared with the comparator? Population: We retrospectively analyzed 837 patients with advanced or metastatic

NSCLC treated with nivolumab across 21 oncology centers in Turkey (2015–

2025). Intervention: Patients with advanced or

metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who received

nivolumab between January 2015 and January 2025 were

included. Comparator: Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS)

were estimated using Kaplan–Meier and compared with log-rank tests. Outcome: Clinical outcomes

The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS),

deﬁned as the time from nivolumab initiation to the ﬁrst

documented disease progression or death from any cause.
claim_text:
PFS was also associated with ECOG performance status

(p < 0.001) and prior thoracic radiotherapy (p = 0.002).

(p < 0.001) and prior thoracic radiotherapy (p = 0.002).
limitations:
This study has several limitations. First, its retrospective

multicenter design introduces risks of selection bias and

heterogeneity in clinical practice patterns across centers. Second,

GLR was measured only at baseline, and dynamic on-treatment

changes—which may offer additional prognostic or predictive

insights for immunotherapy—could not be assessed due to the

retrospective nature of data collection. Third, molecular correlates

such as tumor mutational burden, T-cell clonality, or tumor

microenvironmental characteristics were not available, limiting

our ability to mechanistically validate the observed associations.

In addition, incomplete availability of established biomarkers—

particularly PD-L1 expression and tumor mutational burden—

precluded direct comparative or integrative analyses, limiting

deﬁnitive conclusions regarding the incremental therapeutic

utility of GLR relative to tumor-based or inﬂammation-

derived biomarkers.

Another important limitation is the absence of an external

validation cohort. Although the dataset included patients from 21

institutions, all centers contributed through a uniﬁed national

electronic registry, which prevented the formation of an

independent validation subset. Thus, while the prognostic effect of

GLR remained directionally consistent across multiple clinically

relevant subgroups, external validation in independent populations

is required before clinical implementation. Furthermore, patients in

the high-GLR group more frequently exhibited poorer ECOG

performance status at baseline. Although ECOG was adjusted for

in multivariate analyses, residual confounding related to baseline

functional status cannot be entirely excluded.

Moreover, because GLR incorporates fasting glucose, non–

tumor-related factors—including diabetes mellitus, corticosteroid

exposure, metabolic syndrome, or acute inﬂammation—may

inﬂuence its value. Baseline corticosteroid use was not uniformly

documented across participating centers and therefore could not be

reliably included in multivariate analyses, representing an inherent

limitation of this retrospective real-world dataset. Detailed

metabolic parameters (e.g., HbA1c) and comprehensive

medication histories were not uniformly available across centers,

limiting our ability to adjust for these confounders and representing

an inherent constraint of retrospective real-world datasets.

Similarly, detailed nivolumab exposure data, including exact cycle

numbers, were not consistently recorded across all participating

centers, precluding a reliable cycle-based exposure analysis for the

entire cohort.

Finally, variability in imaging schedules and follow-up intervals

across institutions may have introduced measurement noise,

particularly affecting PFS assessments, despite adherence to

national nivolumab monitoring guidelines. Future prospective

studies with harmonized imaging protocols, standardized

metabolic assessments, and longitudinal GLR measurements—as

survival (OS). ECOG performance status and GLR ≥70.76 were

independent predictors of worse OS, whereas prior thoracic

radiotherapy was associated with improved OS. Hazard ratios (HRs)

are presented with 95% conﬁdence intervals (CIs).

Ersoy et al.

well as multicenter registries speciﬁcally designed for biomarker

validation incorporating external validation cohorts, resampling

techniques (e.g., bootstrapping), and calibration analyses—will be

essential to conﬁrm the reproducibility and generalizability of GLR

as a prognostic biomarker.

Clinical implications

GLR is inexpensive, reproducible, and universally available.

Unlike PD-L1 expression or tumor mutational burden, it requires

no specialized testing and can be obtained repeatedly from routine

blood work. GLR may therefore serve as a practical stratiﬁcation

tool, identifying high-risk patients who warrant closer monitoring,

alternative systemic strategies, or enrollment in clinical trials of

novel combinations.

This study has several limitations. First, its retrospective

multicenter design introduces risks of selection bias and

heterogeneity in clinical practice patterns across centers. Second,

GLR was measured only at baseline, and dynamic on-treatment

changes—which may offer additional prognostic or predictive

insights for immunotherapy—could not be assessed due to the

retrospective nature of data collection. Third, molecular correlates

such as tumor mutational burden, T-cell clonality, or tumor

microenvironmental characteristics were not available, limiting

our ability to mechanistically validate the observed associations.

In addition, incomplete availability of established biomarkers—

particularly PD-L1 expression and tumor mutational burden—

precluded direct comparative or integrative analyses, limiting

deﬁnitive conclusions regarding the incremental therapeutic

utility of GLR relative to tumor-based or inﬂammation-

derived biomarkers.

Another important limitation is the absence of an external

validation cohort. Although the dataset included patients from 21

institutions, all centers contributed through a uniﬁed national

electronic registry, which prevented the formation of an

independent validation subset. Thus, while the prognostic effect of

the high-GLR group more frequently exhibited poorer ECOG

performance status at baseline. Although ECOG was adjusted for

functional status cannot be entirely excluded.

tumor-related factors—including diabetes mellitus, corticosteroid

documented across participating centers and therefore could not be

reliably included in multivariate analyses, representing an inherent

an inherent constraint of retrospective real-world datasets.

centers, precluding a reliable cycle-based exposure analysis for the

entire cohort.

national nivolumab monitoring guidelines. Future prospective

metabolic assessments, and longitudinal GLR measurements—as

result_summary:
Patients Characteristics

In this retrospective series, 62 patients with PIK3CA mutations (n = 56; 90.3%) or

amplifications (n = 6; 9.7%) were included.
limitations:
This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the

findings. First, the retrospective design inherently carries the risk of selection bias and may

have contributed to variability in diagnostic procedures and therapeutic strategies across

participating centers. Owing to the retrospective multicenter design, imaging schedules

and follow-up assessments were not fully standardized across centers, resulting in potential

inter-center heterogeneity in imaging strategies. In addition, reliance on medical records

may have resulted in incomplete capture of certain clinical variables.

The relatively small sample size represents a major limitation, reducing statistical

power and limiting the ability to detect prognostic or predictive effects, particularly in

subgroup analyses. The low number of survival events also limited the feasibility of

multivariable survival analysis.

An additional major limitation is the absence of a matched PIK3CA wild-type control

cohort, which precludes definitive conclusions regarding the independent prognostic

significance of PIK3CA alterations. The frequent coexistence of other oncogenic drivers in

this population further complicates interpretation, as observed outcomes may reflect the

broader molecular context rather than the isolated contribution of PIK3CA status.

Moreover, treatment heterogeneity across disease stages and lines of therapy limits

the interpretability of treatment-specific outcomes and precludes a formal assessment of

predictive value. Systemic therapy choices and radiotherapy approaches were individu-

alized rather than protocol-driven, and detailed information on specific drug regimens,

radiation dose, and treatment fields was not consistently available across centers.

Finally, molecular characterization was restricted to routinely available clinical assays.

Data on mutation clonality, variant allele frequency, and comprehensive downstream PI3K

pathway alterations were not consistently available, precluding a more refined biological

stratification of PIK3CA-altered tumors. In addition, detailed information on the specific

molecular testing methodologies used across centers was not systematically collected.

limitations:
This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the

findings. First, the retrospective design inherently carries the risk of selection bias and may

have contributed to variability in diagnostic procedures and therapeutic strategies across

participating centers. Owing to the retrospective multicenter design, imaging schedules

and follow-up assessments were not fully standardized across centers, resulting in potential

inter-center heterogeneity in imaging strategies. In addition, reliance on medical records

may have resulted in incomplete capture of certain clinical variables.

The relatively small sample size represents a major limitation, reducing statistical

power and limiting the ability to detect prognostic or predictive effects, particularly in

subgroup analyses. The low number of survival events also limited the feasibility of

multivariable survival analysis.

An additional major limitation is the absence of a matched PIK3CA wild-type control

cohort, which precludes definitive conclusions regarding the independent prognostic

significance of PIK3CA alterations. The frequent coexistence of other oncogenic drivers in

this population further complicates interpretation, as observed outcomes may reflect the

broader molecular context rather than the isolated contribution of PIK3CA status.

Moreover, treatment heterogeneity across disease stages and lines of therapy limits

the interpretability of treatment-specific outcomes and precludes a formal assessment of

predictive value. Systemic therapy choices and radiotherapy approaches were individu-

alized rather than protocol-driven, and detailed information on specific drug regimens,

radiation dose, and treatment fields was not consistently available across centers.

Finally, molecular characterization was restricted to routinely available clinical assays.

Data on mutation clonality, variant allele frequency, and comprehensive downstream PI3K

pathway alterations were not consistently available, precluding a more refined biological

stratification of PIK3CA-altered tumors. In addition, detailed information on the specific

molecular testing methodologies used across centers was not systematically collected.

may have resulted in incomplete capture of certain clinical variables.

source_title: Efficacy and safety of Programmed Death Ligand 1 inhibitors versus Programmed Death 1 inhibitors in the first-line treatment of advanced non-small cell lung cancer: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: In a meta-analysis of 28 randomized controlled trials (14,758 patients), PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors combined with chemotherapy improved overall survival compared with chemotherapy alone in the first-line treatment of advanced, driver-mutation-negative NSCLC.
population: Adults with advanced, treatment-naive, driver-mutation-negative non-small cell lung cancer enrolled across 28 included randomized controlled trials of first-line PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitor therapy.
intervention: PD-1 inhibitors (e.g. pembrolizumab, nivolumab, sintilimab, camrelizumab, tislelizumab) or PD-L1 inhibitors (e.g. atezolizumab, durvalumab) combined with platinum-based chemotherapy.
comparator: Chemotherapy alone.
outcome: Overall survival (OS), pooled as hazard ratio across included randomized controlled trials.
result_summary: Compared with chemotherapy alone, PD-L1 inhibitors plus chemotherapy improved OS (HR = 0.82; 95% CI [0.75-0.90]) and PD-1 inhibitors plus chemotherapy improved OS (HR = 0.65; 95% CI [0.61-0.71]). In a separate indirect comparison between the two inhibitor classes when each was combined with chemotherapy, PD-L1 inhibitors were associated with worse OS than PD-1 inhibitors (HR = 1.26; 95% CI [1.13-1.41]; P < 0.001) -- a secondary, class-comparison finding distinct from the primary vs-chemotherapy-alone result this record centers on.

source_span.table_or_figure: Figs. S3 and S4 (supplementary forest plots); indirect PD-L1-vs-PD-1 comparison in Fig. 4B on page 12
source_span.locator_note: The two vs-chemotherapy-alone OS hazard ratios this record centers on (HR=0.82 for PD-L1 inhibitors, HR=0.65 for PD-1 inhibitors, each plus chemotherapy) appear in the 'OS' subsection of Results on document page 5. The secondary PD-L1-vs-PD-1 indirect-comparison HR (1.26) appears on document page 12, continuing the same OS discussion after an intervening full-page figure.

short_source_excerpt: combination treatment with chemotherapy (HR = 0.82; 95% CI [0.75-0.90]) were associated with better OS than chemotherapy alone ... combination treatment with chemotherapy (HR = 0.65; 95% CI [0.61-0.71]) produced better OS than chemotherapy alone
limitations: Manual extraction from one systematic review/meta-analysis only; this record summarizes pooled evidence reported by the review authors rather than reanalyzing individual participant data.
The 28 included RCTs used different specific agents, doses, chemotherapy backbones, and NSCLC histology/PD-L1-expression subpopulations.

The review does not report a pooled statistical-heterogeneity (I-squared) figure for the OS-vs-chemotherapy-alone comparisons in the reviewed text; only the class-vs-class indirect comparison's methodology is described in detail.
This record does not independently assess risk of bias, publication bias, adverse events, durability of response, or overall survival beyond the trials' reported follow-up windows.

The record's primary claim (each class plus chemotherapy vs chemotherapy alone) is distinct from the paper's own headline finding (PD-L1 vs PD-1 class comparison); both are real, source-reported numbers, but a reader should not conflate them.
uncertainty_notes: This evidence bears on the research question by summarizing multiple randomized trials of both PD-1 and PD-L1 inhibitor classes against a shared chemotherapy-alone comparator, but it should be interpreted alongside individual landmark-trial records (not yet present in this corpus's reviewed layer), population/histology subgroup differences, and adverse-event data.

source_title: A Subgroup Analysis of Perioperative Pembrolizumab in Clinical Stage II Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer from the Randomized KEYNOTE-671 Study
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: In the clinical stage II subgroup (n=239) of the phase 3, randomized KEYNOTE-671 trial, perioperative pembrolizumab plus neoadjuvant chemotherapy improved event-free survival and showed a favorable but not statistically significant overall-survival trend compared with neoadjuvant chemotherapy alone.
population: 239 participants with untreated, resectable, clinical stage II NSCLC from the randomized, phase 3 KEYNOTE-671 trial (pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, n=118; chemotherapy alone, n=121); median study follow-up 49.9 months.
intervention: Perioperative pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks plus neoadjuvant chemotherapy for 4 cycles, followed by surgery and adjuvant pembrolizumab for 13 cycles (9 months).
comparator: Placebo plus neoadjuvant chemotherapy for 4 cycles, followed by surgery and adjuvant placebo for 13 cycles.
outcome: Event-free survival (EFS), overall survival (OS), major pathological response (MPR), and pathological complete response (pCR).
result_summary: Event-free survival hazard ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.34-0.74) favored the pembrolizumab arm. Overall survival hazard ratio was 0.69 (95% CI 0.43-1.11) -- directionally favorable but the confidence interval crosses 1, so this stage II subgroup's OS benefit is not independently statistically significant. Major pathological response was 25.7 percentage points higher (95% CI 15.3-35.9) and pathological complete response was 21.3 percentage points higher (95% CI 13.2-30.2) in the pembrolizumab arm. R0 resection occurred in 94.9% (94/99) of the pembrolizumab arm and 86.4% (89/103) of the chemotherapy-alone arm among participants who underwent surgery.

source_span.locator_note: All headline EFS/OS/MPR/pCR figures for this record appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the second PDF page (the paper's own p. 1 body, following a title/graphical-abstract first page).

short_source_excerpt: Event-free survival (hazard ratio [HR], 0.50; 95% CI, 0.34-0.74), overall survival (HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.43-1.11), major pathological response (difference, 25.7%; 95% CI, 15.3-35.9), and pathological complete response (difference, 21.3%; 95% CI, 13.2-30.2) were improved in the pembrolizumab arm.
limitations: This is an exploratory subgroup analysis (clinical stage II only, n=239 of 797 total KEYNOTE-671 participants), not the trial's primary powered analysis population.
The OS hazard ratio's 95% CI crosses 1.0 (0.43-1.11), so OS improvement in this specific subgroup is not independently statistically significant, unlike EFS, MPR, and pCR in the same subgroup.
Grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events were more frequent with pembrolizumab (50.0%) than chemotherapy alone (40.5%); this record does not detail the full safety profile.
Subgroup analyses by clinical stage carry a multiplicity/false-subgroup-finding risk not fully addressed by a single subgroup's point estimate.
This record does not independently assess risk of bias or reanalyze individual patient data; it reports the paper's own subgroup statistics.
uncertainty_notes: This record directly extends the corpus's core question to a perioperative, resectable-disease context and a named real landmark trial (KEYNOTE-671), distinct from the advanced/metastatic first-line setting most other records in this corpus address. The non-significant OS confidence interval should not be read as 'no OS benefit' -- the point estimate and EFS/pathologic-response data are directionally consistent and favorable, but formal OS significance in this subgroup specifically is not established by this analysis alone.

source_title: Overall survival following palliative immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment according to ECOG performance status: a large registry-based study
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: In a large Swedish registry-based real-world cohort, lung cancer patients receiving palliative immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment with a good baseline ECOG performance status (0-1) had substantially longer median overall survival than those with worse baseline performance status (PS 2 or PS 3).
population: 854 lung cancer patients (of 1,956 total patients across multiple cancer types) who received at least one palliative immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment, recorded in Swedish regional Cancer Drug Registries in the Southeastern region, Sweden, from 2010 to April 2025.
intervention: Palliative immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment (single agent or in combination with chemotherapy), assigned at the treating physician's discretion in routine clinical practice (not randomized).
comparator: No concurrent control arm; outcomes compared across baseline ECOG performance-status strata (PS 0-1 vs PS 2 vs PS 3) within the same treated cohort.
outcome: Median overall survival (mOS) from initiation of first palliative ICI treatment, stratified by baseline ECOG performance status.
result_summary: For lung cancer patients, median overall survival was 21.5 months (95% CI 17.5-25.4) in patients with baseline PS 0-1 (n=482, 56.4%), 9.6 months (95% CI 8.1-11.2) in patients with PS 2 (n=320, 37.5%; p<0.001 vs PS 0-1), and 4.3 months (95% CI 2.5-6.1) in patients with PS 3 (n=52, 6.1%; p<0.001 vs PS 0-1). Mortality within 90 days of treatment start was 3.8% for PS 0-1, 20.4% for PS 2, and 40.4% for PS 3 (p<0.001).

source_span.section: Discussion and conclusion (lung-cancer-specific mOS figures) and Table 2 (Median overall survival by diagnosis and ECOG PS)
source_span.locator_note: Table 2 reports mOS by diagnosis (including lung cancer specifically) and PS stratum on the paper's own page 585 (Discussion section, page 4 of the local PDF). The abstract's headline mOS figures (23.4/9.6/3.8 months) are pooled across all cancer types (lung, melanoma, renal, urothelial, etc.), not lung-cancer-specific -- this record deliberately cites the lung-cancer-specific Table 2 values instead of the pooled abstract figures, since this corpus is scoped to NSCLC only.

short_source_excerpt: For lung cancer, we observed a mOS of 9.6 months in patients with PS 2 -- like results from the IPSOS trial -- while patients with PS 3 had a mOS of 4.3 months. Both values were markedly lower than the mOS of 21.5 months observed in patients with PS 0-1.
limitations: Retrospective, registry-based, single-arm real-world cohort with no concurrent non-ICI comparator arm; cannot establish ICI efficacy relative to no treatment or chemotherapy alone.

Not restricted to a single line of therapy, specific histology, PD-L1 expression level, or specific checkpoint-inhibitor agent -- 'lung cancer' here includes any NSCLC (and potentially SCLC; the paper does not state NSCLC-only ascertainment) receiving any palliative ICI regimen at physician discretion.
Selection bias: physicians chose which patients received ICI, and the paper explicitly notes it lacks data on patients not selected for pICI, which could overestimate mOS in the PS>=2 groups.
Kalmar County (one of three regions) ceased recording lung cancer patients to the registry from September 2020 onward, a known data-completeness gap.
No data on prior systemic treatments, comorbidities, immune-related adverse events, healthcare utilization, or quality of life were available in the registry.
uncertainty_notes: This record does not directly compare ICI to a non-ICI comparator; it qualifies the corpus's core question by showing that real-world OS after ICI treatment varies enormously by baseline performance status, a population characteristic largely excluded from the pivotal registration trials (the paper notes only 0.001% of patients in a 35,000-patient RCT meta-analysis had PS >=2). It should be read alongside, not instead of, randomized comparative-efficacy records.

source_title: Composite patient-reported outcomes and risk prediction for overall survival in advanced non-small cell lung cancer with first-line cemiplimab
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: In a secondary analysis of two phase 3 first-line cemiplimab trials (EMPOWER-Lung 1 and EMPOWER-Lung 3), baseline composite patient-reported-outcome burden (combining a functioning scale and a symptom scale) predicted risk of death more strongly than any single patient-reported-outcome scale alone.
population: Patients with advanced NSCLC treated with first-line cemiplimab-based therapy (monotherapy or plus chemotherapy) in the EMPOWER-Lung 1 and EMPOWER-Lung 3 phase 3 trials; baseline patient-reported-outcome analyses included approximately 590-593 patients depending on the specific scale.
intervention: First-line cemiplimab (anti-PD-1), as monotherapy (EMPOWER-Lung 1) or combined with chemotherapy (EMPOWER-Lung 3), stratified by baseline EORTC QLQ-C30/QLQ-LC13 patient-reported-outcome burden.
comparator: Within-cohort comparison of high- versus low-risk baseline composite PRO burden groups among cemiplimab-treated patients; not a comparison against a non-ICI treatment arm.
outcome: Overall survival (OS), modeled via Cox proportional-hazards regression using baseline PRO burden as the predictor, stratified by treatment, histology, and PD-L1 level.
result_summary: The strongest composite PRO predictor of OS was baseline social functioning combined with lung-cancer-specific dyspnea burden: hazard ratio 2.52 (95% CI 1.75-3.64, P<.001, n=591 at risk). All of the top 10 composite PRO measures had HR >=2 and P<.05, versus the strongest single-scale PRO (social functioning alone), which had a lower HR of 1.92 (95% CI 1.43-2.58, P<.001, n=593). Patients with low functioning and high symptom burden at baseline had worse OS than those with high functioning and low symptom burden.

source_span.locator_note: Table 3 ('Top 10 overall survival HRs of composite and single PROs at baseline from a Cox proportional model') appears on the fourth page of the local PDF (the paper's own page 4) and contains the exact composite and single-PRO hazard ratios this record reports.

limitations: This is a prognostic/risk-prediction analysis within cemiplimab-treated patients, not a comparison of cemiplimab against a non-ICI comparator -- it does not itself demonstrate that checkpoint inhibitors improve OS versus an alternative treatment.

Baseline PRO burden is a patient-reported measure, potentially confounded by underlying disease severity, comorbidities, or unmeasured prognostic factors that this record's Cox model cannot fully disentangle from a direct causal PRO effect.

The composite PRO risk-stratification approach was developed and evaluated on the same trial data (EMPOWER-Lung 1 and EMPOWER-Lung 3); the paper does not report external validation in an independent cohort.
Multiple composite PRO combinations were tested (a multiplicity concern common to top-10-of-many-combinations reporting), which the paper does not explicitly correct for.
This record does not assess the composite PRO measure's clinical utility for treatment decision-making, only its statistical association with OS.
uncertainty_notes: This record qualifies the corpus's core question by showing that within a checkpoint-inhibitor-treated population, baseline patient-reported functional/symptom burden -- not treatment assignment itself -- is a strong OS predictor. It should not be read as evidence for or against ICI efficacy relative to a comparator; it complements comparative-efficacy records by identifying a real prognostic factor among ICI-treated patients.

source_title: Durvalumab Consolidation After Definitive Chemoradiotherapy in Patients with Unresectable Stage III Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Real-World Cohort Analysis from the German Prospective, Observational CRISP Registry (AIO-TRK-0315)
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: In a real-world, propensity-weighted cohort from the German CRISP registry, durvalumab consolidation after chemoradiotherapy in unresectable stage III NSCLC significantly improved progression-free survival and showed a favorable but not statistically significant overall-survival trend, with effect sizes comparable to the PACIFIC trial.
population: 231 patients with unresectable stage III NSCLC enrolled in the prospective, multicenter CRISP registry in Germany (August 2018-June 2023): 124 treated with durvalumab consolidation, 107 without.
intervention: Durvalumab consolidation therapy after definitive chemoradiotherapy (87% received concurrent chemoradiotherapy).
comparator: Chemoradiotherapy without durvalumab consolidation.
outcome: Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), assessed after stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW).
result_summary: In the weighted analysis, median PFS was significantly longer with durvalumab consolidation (18.6 months, 95% CI [12.8, 24.5] vs. 7.5 months, 95% CI [5.5, 8.4]; HR 0.52, 95% CI [0.37, 0.73]). source_title: Genomic biomarkers of immunotherapy plus chemotherapy in patients with advanced NSCLC: Insights from the phase 3 ORIENT-11 study
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: A 9-gene immune-chemotherapy prediction score (ICPscore), derived from RNA-seq data of patients in the phase 3 ORIENT-11 trial, identifies a subgroup of advanced NSCLC patients who derive substantial progression-free and overall-survival benefit from sintilimab (anti-PD-1) plus chemotherapy over chemotherapy alone, while patients below the score's median show no significant benefit.
population: Advanced NSCLC patients from the phase 3 ORIENT-11 trial (sintilimab plus pemetrexed/platinum vs. pemetrexed/platinum alone, N=397 in the trial), with a discovery/validation subset of 171 patients (high-ICPscore n=85, low-ICPscore n=86) used for the survival-stratification analysis reported here; the ICPscore was further validated in independent OAK (N=699) and IMvigor210 (N=192, urothelial carcinoma) cohorts.
intervention: Sintilimab (anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor) plus pemetrexed/platinum chemotherapy, stratified by baseline high vs. low ICPscore.
comparator: Pemetrexed/platinum chemotherapy alone, within the same ICPscore stratum.
outcome: Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), compared between ICI-chemotherapy and chemotherapy-alone arms, separately within high- and low-ICPscore subgroups.
result_summary: High-ICPscore patients receiving ICI-chemotherapy had superior PFS (HR = 0.15, 95% CI [0.07, 0.32], p < 0.0001) and OS (HR = 0.32, 95% CI [0.15, 0.67], p = 0.0002) compared with chemotherapy alone. Low-ICPscore patients showed no significant PFS benefit (HR = 0.90, 95% CI [0.55, 1.46], p = 0.661) and no significant OS benefit (HR = 1.31, 95% CI [0.81, 2.12], p = 0.294) from adding ICI to chemotherapy.

limitations: The ICPscore is a novel, single-study-derived 9-gene signature; while validated in OAK and IMvigor210, IMvigor210 is a urothelial-carcinoma (bladder cancer) cohort, not NSCLC, so its validation strength for this corpus's NSCLC-specific question is partial.

source_title: Comparison of real-world efficacy and safety of nivolumab plus ipilimumab or pembrolizumab combined with platinum-based chemotherapy in advanced non-small cell lung cancer
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: In a real-world, single-center German cohort, nivolumab plus ipilimumab with platinum-based chemotherapy (NIC) and pembrolizumab with platinum-based chemotherapy (PC) showed no statistically significant difference in overall survival or time to treatment discontinuation, though the two regimens differed in their adverse-event profiles.
population: 200 patients with advanced NSCLC treated between July 2018 and June 2023 at a single German center: 77 treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab plus chemotherapy (NIC), 123 treated with pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy (PC). Baseline characteristics were unbalanced, with significantly more older, squamous-histology, and PD-L1-negative patients in the NIC group.
intervention: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab (dual checkpoint inhibition) combined with platinum-based chemotherapy.
comparator: Pembrolizumab (single anti-PD-1) combined with platinum-based chemotherapy.
outcome: Overall survival (OS) and time to treatment discontinuation (TTD), the study's primary endpoints; clinically significant adverse events as a secondary endpoint.
result_summary: Median OS was not significantly different between NIC and PC (13.6 vs. 14.1 months). Median TTD was also similar (5.8 vs. 6.2 months). Clinically significant adverse events, related treatment discontinuations, and treatment-related deaths did not differ significantly (p=0.885/p=1.000/p=0.709 respectively). Immune-related adverse events were more frequent in the NIC group (p=0.001); chemotherapy-related adverse events were more frequent in the PC group (p<0.001).

source_span.locator_note: The OS/TTD comparison and adverse-event p-values this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: Median overall survival (OS) and time to treatment discontinuation (TTD) were not significantly different in the NIC and PC groups (13.6 vs. 14.1 months / 5.8 vs. 6.2 months).
limitations: Retrospective, single-center, non-randomized comparison between two active regimens (not a comparison against chemotherapy alone); baseline characteristics were explicitly unbalanced between groups (more older, squamous, PD-L1-negative patients in the NIC group), and the analysis does not report a formal adjustment (e.g. propensity weighting) for these imbalances.
Modest sample size (200 total, 77 vs 123), especially for the NIC arm, limiting power to detect a true OS difference if one exists.
The paper's own conclusion explicitly states 'further analyses are needed to validate our findings.'
This record does not independently assess risk of bias or reanalyze the adverse-event classification methodology.
This is a comparison between two active ICI-based regimens, not a comparison against a non-ICI comparator, so it does not itself demonstrate ICI efficacy versus chemotherapy alone.

source_title: Real-World Long-Term Outcomes of First-Line Pembrolizumab in Advanced PD-L1 >= 50% NSCLC: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 real-world studies (17,506 patients) found that first-line pembrolizumab monotherapy in advanced NSCLC with PD-L1 >= 50% produced durable long-term survival, with outcomes closely mirroring pivotal-trial results, and identified older age and poor performance status as predictors of worse survival.
population: 17,506 patients with advanced NSCLC and PD-L1 expression >= 50% (excluding EGFR/ALK-altered tumors), pooled across 12 real-world studies identified via systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library through February 2025.
intervention: First-line pembrolizumab monotherapy.
comparator: None (single-arm pooled real-world outcomes, not a comparative analysis against chemotherapy or another regimen); comparison is against pivotal-trial benchmarks in the discussion, not a formal statistical comparator arm.
outcome: Pooled mean overall survival (OS), 60-month OS rate, progression-free survival (PFS), adverse-event rates, and OS hazard ratios by age, ECOG performance status, PD-L1 intensity, and brain metastases.
result_summary: Pooled mean OS was 21.0 months (95% CI 16.9-25.1); 60-month OS rate was 29.0%. Mean PFS was 8.7 months (95% CI 6.3-11.0). Any-grade and grade >=3 adverse events occurred in 52% and 12% of patients respectively. Age >=70 years was associated with worse OS (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.23-1.29). ECOG status >=2 was associated with worse OS (HR 2.05, 95% CI 1.04-4.05). No significant OS difference was observed by PD-L1 intensity (within the >=50% band) or by presence of brain metastases.

source_span.locator_note: The pooled OS/PFS figures and subgroup hazard ratios this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: The pooled mean OS was 21.0 months (95% confidence interval [CI] 16.9-25.1), and the 60-month OS rate was 29.0%. Mean progression-free survival was 8.7 months (95% CI 6.3-11.0).
limitations: This is a single-arm pooled analysis of real-world cohorts, not a comparison against chemotherapy alone or another regimen; it demonstrates durability of pembrolizumab monotherapy's real-world effect, not comparative superiority.
Pooling 12 real-world studies introduces heterogeneity in patient selection, follow-up duration, and outcome-ascertainment methodology that a pooled mean does not fully capture.
Kaplan-Meier curves were digitally reconstructed from published figures using R, an indirect data-extraction method with inherent imprecision compared with access to individual patient data.
This record does not independently assess publication bias, study-quality weighting, or risk-of-bias across the 12 included studies.
The population is deliberately narrow (PD-L1 >=50%, EGFR/ALK-negative), so this record's findings do not generalize to lower PD-L1 expression or driver-mutation-positive populations.

source_title: Real-World Survival Outcomes Following Chemoradiotherapy with or Without Durvalumab in PD-L1-Defined Subgroups of Stage III Unresectable Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: In a real-world, single-center retrospective cohort, durvalumab consolidation after chemoradiotherapy significantly improved overall survival and progression-free survival in PD-L1-positive patients with unresectable stage III NSCLC, while PD-L1-negative patients showed no significant survival difference regardless of durvalumab use.
population: 142 patients with inoperable stage III NSCLC treated with definitive chemoradiotherapy between 2015 and 2022 at a single center; mean follow-up 44.0 months. Assigned to three cohorts by PD-L1 status and durvalumab use: PD-L1-positive with durvalumab maintenance (n=57), PD-L1-positive without durvalumab (n=44), and PD-L1-negative without durvalumab (n=41).
intervention: Durvalumab consolidation/maintenance therapy after definitive chemoradiotherapy, in PD-L1-positive patients.
comparator: Chemoradiotherapy without durvalumab consolidation, compared within PD-L1-positive patients and separately in PD-L1-negative patients.
outcome: Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), compared across the three PD-L1/durvalumab-defined cohorts.
result_summary: Median OS was 27.3, 15.1, and 23.4 months for PD-L1-positive-with-durvalumab, PD-L1-positive-without-durvalumab, and PD-L1-negative-without-durvalumab respectively; median PFS was 18.4, 10.5, and 13.4 months respectively. OS and PFS were significantly improved with durvalumab in PD-L1-positive patients (p=0.043 and p=0.027). PD-L1-negative patients showed no significant OS or PFS difference versus PD-L1-positive patients who did not receive durvalumab. Immunotherapy-related pneumonitis of grade >=1 occurred in 15.7% of durvalumab-treated patients.

source_span.locator_note: The three-cohort median OS/PFS figures and p-values this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: OS and PFS were significantly improved with durvalumab in PD-L1-positive patients (p = 0.043 and p = 0.027). PD-L1-negative patients showed no significant OS or PFS differences versus PD-L1+oD.
limitations: Retrospective, single-center, non-randomized cohort with small subgroup sizes (41-57 patients per arm), limiting statistical power, particularly for the PD-L1-negative comparison.
PD-L1 testing included retrospective testing for some patients, which the paper does not detail as being blinded to outcome or performed uniformly with prospectively-tested patients.

This record does not independently assess why some PD-L1-positive patients did not receive durvalumab (selection factors such as toxicity from chemoradiotherapy, disease progression, or clinician/patient choice are not detailed here), a real confounding-by-indication risk.

This is real-world observational data, not a randomized comparison; the PACIFIC trial itself (the RCT establishing durvalumab consolidation as standard of care) is not in this corpus (closed-access venue, no PMC OA record).

The PD-L1-negative subgroup finding (no significant difference) should not be read as proof of no benefit in that subgroup given the small sample size.

source_title: Efficacy of first-line treatment in driver gene-negative non-small cell lung cancer with liver metastases: a Bayesian network meta-analysis
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: In a Bayesian network meta-analysis of 20 randomized controlled trials, PD-1 inhibitor plus chemotherapy significantly improved progression-free survival and overall survival compared with chemotherapy alone, in treatment-naive, driver-gene-negative NSCLC patients with liver metastases.
population: Treatment-naive adults with driver gene-negative NSCLC and liver metastases, enrolled across 20 included randomized controlled trials of first-line treatment (PROSPERO CRD42025632364).
intervention: PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor plus chemotherapy (various regimens, including camrelizumab plus chemotherapy).
comparator: Chemotherapy alone.
outcome: Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), pooled as hazard ratios via Bayesian network meta-analysis; SUCRA ranking across regimens.
result_summary: PD-1 inhibitor plus chemotherapy significantly improved PFS (HR 0.572, 95% CI [0.435, 0.754]) and OS (HR 0.681, 95% CI [0.559, 0.830]) compared with chemotherapy alone. In patients with squamous NSCLC specifically, PD-1 inhibitor plus chemotherapy also showed a significant PFS benefit over chemotherapy alone (HR 0.583, 95% CI [0.386, 0.882]). Camrelizumab plus chemotherapy ranked highest among all evaluated regimens for both PFS (SUCRA 84.18%) and OS (SUCRA 96.38%). The authors caution that these are indirect-comparison findings from a network meta-analysis, not head-to-head trial results.

source_span.locator_note: The PFS/OS hazard ratios, confidence intervals, and SUCRA rankings this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: PD-1 inhibitor plus chemotherapy significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) (HR = 0.572, 95% CI: 0.435-0.754) and overall survival (OS) (HR = 0.681, 95% CI: 0.559-0.830) compared with chemotherapy alone.
limitations: This is a subpopulation-specific meta-analysis (driver gene-negative NSCLC with liver metastases specifically), not a general-population NSCLC result -- findings should not be generalized to NSCLC patients without liver metastases without caution.

A Bayesian network meta-analysis relies on indirect comparisons across trials with different specific agents, chemotherapy backbones, and patient subpopulations; the authors themselves caution these findings should be 'interpreted with caution' given the indirect-comparison design.

The camrelizumab-plus-chemotherapy SUCRA ranking is a probabilistic best-treatment ranking, not a statistically significant head-to-head superiority claim over other PD-1/PD-L1-plus-chemotherapy regimens.
This record does not independently assess the meta-analysis's risk-of-bias assessment, heterogeneity statistics, or publication-bias handling beyond what the abstract reports.

source_title: Antibody-based regimens targeting PD-1/PD-L1 and VEGF/VEGFR in advanced or metastatic NSCLC: a meta-analysis of RCTs
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: In a meta-analysis of 11 randomized controlled trials (4,426 participants), antibody-based regimens combining PD-1/PD-L1 inhibition with VEGF/VEGFR-targeting antibodies, with or without chemotherapy, significantly improved progression-free survival and overall survival compared with control regimens in advanced or metastatic NSCLC.
population: Adults with advanced or metastatic NSCLC enrolled across 11 included randomized controlled trials (4,426 participants total), registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251126421).
intervention: Antibody-based regimens targeting PD-1/PD-L1 and VEGF/VEGFR: conventional PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors combined with anti-angiogenic monoclonal antibodies, or PD-1/VEGF or PD-L1/VEGF bispecific antibodies, with or without chemotherapy.
comparator: Control regimen (not combining PD-1/PD-L1 and VEGF/VEGFR targeting).
outcome: Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), pooled as hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals across included randomized controlled trials, with prespecified clinicopathological subgroup analyses.
result_summary: Antibody-based regimens targeting PD-1/PD-L1 and VEGF/VEGFR were associated with better PFS (HR 0.65, 95% CI [0.57, 0.75], p<0.001) and OS (HR 0.79, 95% CI [0.71, 0.87], p<0.001) compared with control regimens. Favorable PFS subgroup estimates were observed in men (HR 0.61), squamous histology (HR 0.57), patients with liver metastases (HR 0.49), high PD-L1 expression (TPS >= 50%: HR 0.65), and EGFR-mutant patients (HR 0.60). Favorable OS subgroup estimates were observed in ECOG performance status 1 (HR 0.80), men (HR 0.80), smokers (HR 0.82), liver metastases (HR 0.57), PD-L1 TPS 1-49% (HR 0.67), and EGFR-mutant patients (HR 0.80).

source_span.locator_note: The pooled PFS/OS hazard ratios, confidence intervals, p-values, and clinicopathological subgroup hazard ratios this record centers on appear in the paper's structured Abstract on the first page of the local PDF.

short_source_excerpt: Antibody-based regimens targeting PD-1/PD-L1 and VEGF/VEGFR, with or without chemotherapy, were associated with better PFS (HR = 0.65, 95%CI: 0.57-0.75, p<0.001) and OS (HR = 0.79, 95%CI: 0.71-0.87, p<0.001) compared with the control regimen.
limitations: This meta-analysis pools multiple distinct antibody combinations (conventional PD-1/PD-L1 plus anti-angiogenic antibodies, and bispecific PD-1/VEGF or PD-L1/VEGF antibodies) rather than isolating any single regimen's effect, so the pooled hazard ratios should not be attributed to any specific agent without checking the paper's per-regimen subgroup analyses.

The clinicopathological subgroup hazard ratios (by sex, histology, metastasis site, PD-L1 expression, EGFR mutation status) are secondary/exploratory findings from the pooled trials, not prespecified primary comparisons within each individual RCT.
This record does not independently assess the meta-analysis's risk-of-bias assessment, heterogeneity statistics, or publication-bias handling beyond what the abstract reports.
The 11 included RCTs likely differ in specific agents, doses, and chemotherapy backbones, which this abstract-level summary does not fully capture.

source_title: Induction Chemoimmunotherapy Followed by Consolidative Hypofractionated Radiotherapy for Unresectable Locally Advanced NSCLC: A Real-World Outcomes Analysis
research_question: Do immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) improve overall survival in adults with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)?
claim_text: In a real-world retrospective cohort, induction chemoimmunotherapy followed by consolidative hypofractionated radiotherapy was associated with favorable locoregional control, encouraging 1- and 2-year survival outcomes, and acceptable toxicity in patients with unresectable locally advanced NSCLC.
population: 34 patients with unresectable locally advanced NSCLC (LA-NSCLC), treated between 2019 and 2025; median age 64 years, median PD-L1 expression 20%; squamous cell carcinoma (56%) and adenocarcinoma (38%) were predominant histologies.
intervention: Induction chemoimmunotherapy (most commonly carboplatin/paclitaxel plus nivolumab, median 4 cycles) followed by consolidative hypofractionated radiotherapy (median 52.5 Gy in 15 fractions); maintenance immunotherapy administered in 79% of patients.
comparator: None (single-arm real-world retrospective cohort; outcomes reported descriptively, not against a comparator arm).
outcome: Primary: local recurrence. Secondary: regional recurrence, distant metastasis, overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and treatment-related toxicity, at a median follow-up of 16.7 months.
result_summary: Post-induction response was complete in 21%, partial in 62%, stable in 12%, and progressive in 6%. Using cumulative incidence functions with death as a competing event, 1- and 2-year cumulative incidences were: local failure 6.9% and 14.7%; regional failure 10.2% and 18.8%; distant metastasis 15.9% and 39.2%. No isolated local or regional recurrences occurred. One- and two-year OS rates were 86% and 81%; corresponding PFS rates were 76% and 54%. No grade 4-5 radiotherapy-related toxicity occurred; one grade 5 immune-related pneumonitis was observed.

source_span.locator_note: The response rates, cumulative-incidence figures, and OS/PFS rates this record centers on appear in the Results portion of the paper's structured Abstract, continuing onto page 2 of the local PDF from the Simple Summary/Abstract heading on page 1.

short_source_excerpt: One- and two-year OS rates were 86% and 81%, and corresponding PFS rates were 76% and 54%. No grade 4-5 RT-related toxicity occurred; one grade 5 immune-related pneumonitis was observed.
limitations: Very small sample size (n=34) from a single-arm retrospective real-world cohort at two affiliated centers, without a comparator arm -- these outcomes cannot be attributed to any specific component of the treatment sequence (induction chemoimmunotherapy vs consolidative radiotherapy vs maintenance immunotherapy) in isolation.

Retrospective design introduces selection bias (patients selected for this treatment sequence based on multidisciplinary tumor board judgment) and potential incomplete toxicity capture relative to a prospective trial.

A predominantly squamous-histology cohort (56%) with a specific real-world PD-L1 and induction-regimen profile; findings should not be generalized to other histology distributions or induction regimens without caution.

This record does not independently assess follow-up completeness, competing-risk model assumptions, or missing-data handling beyond what the paper reports; median follow-up of 16.7 months is relatively short for durable 2-year estimates.
uncertainty_notes: This record supports the corpus's core question by demonstrating favorable real-world outcomes for a sequential immunotherapy-containing treatment strategy in unresectable LA-NSCLC, but as a small, single-arm, uncontrolled cohort it carries much weaker evidentiary weight than this corpus's randomized controlled trial and meta-analysis records -- it should be read as real-world feasibility/hypothesis-generating evidence, not confirmatory efficacy evidence.
